pages.title: How import works
pages.blurb: What we accept, how files are classified, viewing and downloading originals, the quality checks, questionnaire links, statistical output sets, wave comparison, and where they stop

sections.heading: Introduction
sections.text:
How import works
What happens to a file between upload and analysis: how it is read, checked and accepted, how a questionnaire or guide is attached, and how a set of statistical output (models, clusters, diagnostics) becomes checked findings. It describes current behaviour and will change as the app does.
Method guides · about 16 minute read · updated 2026-10-22

sections.heading: What Import is for
sections.text:
Import is the step where material is looked at before anything is built on it. Most problems in a finished analysis were visible at this stage: a weight variable that is empty for a fifth of the file, a transcript that is mostly the moderator talking, a table whose percentages do not add to 100, an odds ratio file that comes from a different model run than the coefficients beside it. The aim is to show these early, in plain words, while they are cheap to fix. The thinking behind it is the total survey error view: a result can be wrong for many reasons besides sampling, and the reasons are easiest to catch where the data enters (Groves & Lyberg, 2010).
How well a file reads depends a good deal on how it is laid out. The guide to preparing your files gives layout tips for each kind.
Import does not decide whether the evidence is good enough. It reports what it found, with the figures, and leaves the judgement to you.

sections.heading: What you can bring, and what each kind gets
sections.text:
Kind | What it is | What Import does with it
Report | A narrative document, deck or PDF that makes claims | Reads it and extracts atomic claims for verification (see the findings guide).
Data file | Case-level data (.sav, .dta, .csv, .xlsx; SAS excluded pending verification) or an already summarised table | Case-level files are read, checked and held for the cross tab tool. Summarised tables get their own table checks and can generate findings.
Transcript | An interview or group discussion | Checks it before coding: who speaks, how much, how the moderator behaves, and whether it is long enough to code.
Questionnaire or guide | The instrument behind the data or the discussion | Attached to a data file or to transcripts, read automatically, and matched. See below.
Statistical output | A zip or several files of model results, cluster profiles, diagnostics and logs | Sorted into a set, classified, checked as a set, and turned into findings. See below.
Cross tabulations are not imported as output. Any case-level data goes through the cross tab tool, which weights, tests and labels it consistently. Statistical output is for everything else a statistician produces around the data.

sections.heading: Reading and accepting data files
sections.text:
A case-level data file is read as soon as it arrives. The read gets the variable list, labels, value labels and the structure choices (which variable is the weight, which identify respondents, which are multiple response sets). You do not have to press anything for this to happen. The file is also accepted automatically, so the cross tab tool opens without a trip back to Import.
Transcripts follow the same rule. A transcript nobody has set up yet is accepted on import with the app's best reading of it (individual interviews when it cannot tell), and the dropdowns stay open to change it. Every file card now shows one of two badges: Accepted or Needs review. Raw case-level files are labelled Raw data on the card and in the upload list. The upload list puts each file picker on the same line as its type to save space, and a note under it says that you should upload only files that the owner has cleared for analysis, since the app does not scan for personal information.
Acceptance is a record that the structure was looked at, not a verdict on the data. If you change a structure choice afterwards, the card changes to Accept again, because tables built on the old choice may no longer mean what they did. Wide files, with thousands of columns, keep only the usable variables, and the panel says how many were kept; the cross tab tool still reads every variable it needs.
The file list and the selected file
The list of sources rolls up with its own button, which only hides it: the search, filters and sort keep their state. Each file names its links on its type and date line ("Linked: questionnaire.docx", and "and N more"), so you can see what is linked without opening it. The selected file shows its name on one line and its type, upload date, wave and purpose on the next. Raw data offers Open Crosstabs and Open Analytics; a summarised table offers Open Crosstabs only, because Analytics needs case-level data.
View original downloads the file exactly as it was uploaded, under its own name, without opening a window. Viewing opens a readable copy in a browser tab where there is one (a PDF). Both use a short-lived link, checked on the server to belong to this project; it stops working after ten minutes. If a download fails, the reason shows under the button and pressing it again tries again. The original file is never changed.
Why it works this way
Accepting by default saves a step nearly everyone would take anyway. Asking again after a change keeps the one safeguard that matters: a table should never silently rest on a different structure than the one you approved.

sections.heading: What the quality panels check
sections.text:
Each card has a rolled-up quality panel. It reports figures, not scores, so you can see why it says what it says. The table of checks is rolled up by default; its summary line gives the number of checks, how many passed, how many to check and how many have a problem, with the worst status beside it.
Case-level data
- Missing values. How much is empty, per variable. Survey routing creates legitimate gaps: a person never asked a question is not a non-response. Where one variable cleanly splits empty from answered (a gate question), the gaps it explains are set aside and the file reports what is left once routed questions are accounted for.
- Weights. Whether a weight variable is present, how many cases lack a weight, and how variable the weights are. Very unequal weights reduce the effective sample size. This has its own Weights tab.
- Missing-value codes. Codes for don't know, refused and not applicable, in a fold under Variables. The fold reads the file when you open it. The detection rules are the same as before; only the place changed.
- Value labels. A row in the checks table gives the exact number of variables in the label sheets that are not in the data (their labels are not applied), with every name in a fold, and the number with conflicting labels. It is a note: it does not change the table's status.
- Structure. Duplicated respondents, constant columns, label look-alikes, and codes that look like missing values but are not flagged.
Summarised tables
- Tables read, whether a base is stated for each, and whether any base is under 30 or under 10.
- Whether weighting is stated, whether percentage columns add to about 100, and whether counts agree with the total row.
- Duplicate tables, extraction damage (merged cells, split headers) and column layouts the reader had to guess.
Transcripts
- Respondents, turns, and words per respondent, with thin respondents named.
- Moderator share of the talk, dominant voices, and quiet members of a group.
- Questions asked, split into open, closed and leading, and how long the answers were.
- Inaudible markers, duplicated turns, very long turns, speaker labels that look alike, and whether there are timestamps.
Limitation: Checks find signs, not causes
A high share of missing values can mean a routing gap, a bad export, or a real pattern of refusal. The panel cannot tell which. The same is true of a moderator who talks a lot: that may be a weak interview or a deliberately directive one. Treat each line as a prompt to look.

sections.heading: Questionnaires and guides
sections.text:
A questionnaire sits inside the data file card, and a guide inside the transcript card, rolled up. They are read automatically when they arrive, and the wrong one can be removed with the delete button beside it.
Questionnaire
The read produces a list of items: code, wording, answer options and any printed skip instruction. Matching to the data then proceeds from the most to the least reliable signal: same code, same code stem (Q12 to Q12_1; Q1 never matches Q10), a variable label that starts with the code, and last, overlapping wording. Every match starts as a suggestion with its method and confidence. You can confirm a whole batch of same-code matches at once, or accept and reject them one by one.
Confirmed matches do three things.
- They supply the full question wording as a tooltip and as a variable label, and answer labels where the data file has none. The data file's own labels always win. Rejecting a match takes effect at once, because the stored dictionary is not changed.
- They supply skip logic. Printed instructions such as "ASK IF Q5 = 1 or 2" and jumps on answer options ("GO TO Q10") are read into rules. A rule is used to separate people who were not asked from people who skipped only if at least 90% of the cases it says were not asked are in fact empty; otherwise the detected routing is the fallback.
- They can later give wording for the labels in a statistical output set (see below).
Codes the questionnaire marks as don't know are treated as missing once a link is confirmed, so bases and percentages can change. A note on the data file's links tab and on the questionnaire says so. Nothing applies until a link is confirmed, and the data file itself is never changed. The card counts these as "Question and variable links confirmed".
A multiple-response heading question (such as EN20, with the data in EN20_1 to EN20_12) has no single variable of its own. When no variable has the code itself, the variables named the code plus a separator and a suffix are suggested together as its family, and "Confirm same-code matches" can confirm them. By hand, "Choose variable" offers "Link all N" for the family. The separator is the boundary: EN2 never takes EN20_1, and EN20 never takes EN201. Linked to a family, the question only adds its wording as a tooltip; the members keep their own answer labels.
Guide
Moderator questions in each transcript are split out and compared with the guide items by wording overlap. A question counts as asked at an overlap of 0.7 or more, reworded from 0.4 to 0.7, and the rest as not asked. Per session you see items raised, items not raised, and moderator questions outside the guide (probes are expected). Coverage of 80% or more reads as a pass, 50% to 80% as a check. Up to 25 guide topics are also passed to the open-coding step as hints, worded so that a theme still needs support in the transcript.
Limitation: Wording overlap is a rough measure
A moderator can ask a guide question in words that share little with the printed wording, and two different questions can share many words. Coverage figures are a first look at fidelity to the guide, not a score for the moderator.

sections.heading: Statistical output sets
sections.text:
Model coefficients, odds ratios, cluster profiles, diagnostics and the logs that explain them usually arrive as a folder of files from R, SPSS, Stata or Python. Upload them as one zip, or select several files, and give the study or wave a label. They become one output set. Images are left out, and very large or deeply nested uploads are limited (up to 400 files, 40 MB for a file, 300 MB for the set).
Each file is sorted by what it contains, with the signals shown, so the sort can be checked. There are two questions. First, what role does it play?
Role | Meaning | Examples
Evidence | Findings are built from it | Coefficients, odds ratios, proportions with intervals, cluster profiles
Assurance | Says how far to trust the evidence | Diagnostics, design effects, collinearity, separation, replication and robustness checks
Context | Explains how the output was produced | Run manifests, survey design records, session information, author notes, the console log
To check | No clear pattern was found | Anything the sorter could not place
Second, what kind of file is it? The kinds include model coefficients, odds ratios and intervals, proportions with intervals, cluster profiles, descriptive tables, diagnostics, validation checks, and the context kinds above. Files are grouped into families for the roll-down, by folder or by a shared first word of the name.
Example
An R script writes DV1_Model1_coefficients.csv and DV1_Model1_ORs.csv, a GVIF summary, a design-effect table, a folder of robustness runs with an exact-replication check, and a Word copy of the console. The sorter treats the first two as evidence, the next three and the replication check as assurance, and the console copy as context. If a script did not write something to a file but it appears in the console (for example which category was left out as the reference), the console copy is how the app recovers it.

sections.heading: The checks on an output set
sections.text:
Check this set compares the files with each other and reads the assurance files. It writes no findings. The results stay on the set card, with a green, amber or grey marker for each.
Check | What it asks | Why it matters
Odds ratios equal exp(estimate) | For each paired model, does every odds ratio equal the exponential of its coefficient? | A mismatch means the two files come from different model runs, a common slip when files are regenerated one at a time.
Intervals fit the standard errors | Does the width of each odds ratio interval imply a critical value near 1.96? | A different value points to another confidence level or degrees of freedom than the standard errors suggest.
Test statistics fit estimate over standard error | Is each t or z value within 1% of estimate divided by standard error? | Catches columns pasted from a different model.
Published results reproduce | Did every row of a replication or validation file pass? | A failed row means the headline numbers may not be the ones in the report.
Separation | Did any model flag quasi-complete separation? | Under separation the estimates can run away to very large values and cannot be trusted (Albert & Anderson, 1984; Heinze & Schemper, 2002).
Collinearity | How large is the biggest adjusted generalised variance inflation factor? | Adjusted GVIF is on the scale of a standard error inflation; values from about 2.24 deserve a look and from about 3.16 are a concern. These are rules of thumb, not tests (Fox & Monette, 1992).
Design effect | What design effect does the output report? | It says how much less precise the complex sample makes an estimate than a simple random sample of the same size.
Small cells | How many unweighted cases are in the smallest outcome cell? | Under 30 is a caution and under 10 a concern.
Robustness across specifications | Do headline terms keep their direction, and an interval excluding 1, in every alternative model? | A term that flips in some specifications may owe its result to a modelling choice.
Reference categories | Does the console log state which level was left out? | An odds ratio means nothing without the group it is compared with.
Limitation: Consistency is not correctness
The checks show that the files agree with each other and with the usual conventions. They cannot show that the model was the right one, that the weights were right, or that the script did what the author intended.

sections.heading: From output to findings
sections.text:
Make findings reads each evidence file with a reader that fits its kind and writes one finding per model, table or segment variable. Running it again replaces the findings from that set.
- Models. One finding per model. It says how many terms reached p < .05 and describes the four clearest, ranked by test statistic, with odds ratio, interval and p value. Where the reference category is known from the console log, the text says what the odds are compared with. Odds ratios that are extreme with very wide intervals, which usually mean very few cases in a group, are left out of the summary and counted. If no term reaches p < .05, the finding says so.
- Interaction and odds ratio tables. One finding per block, with the same treatment of extreme ratios. A non-significant interaction is reported as little evidence of a difference, not as evidence of none.
- Segments. Proportions with intervals give a finding only where the highest and lowest groups have separate intervals. Estimates with standard errors are compared by the size of the gap against the combined standard error.
- Clusters. The finding names the variables on which the clusters differ most, with group sizes, and attaches the silhouette width when a file reports it (Rousseeuw, 1987).
Every finding carries assurance notes from the set. Cautions and checks show on the finding; the rest are rolled up beneath it. Typical notes are the design effect, collinearity, separation, that p values are not adjusted for the number of terms, that a reference category is not stated, that a segment gap rests on separate intervals and not a formal test, and the robustness record for the same term.
Robustness and sensitivity files, such as a folder of alternative specifications, are not turned into findings of their own. They feed the robustness check and the notes on the headline findings. Descriptive tables with no interval or test are listed as read but giving no finding.
Why it works this way
A model finding that does not carry its own warnings travels badly. A figure pasted into a deck loses the design effect, the unadjusted p value and the reference category that gave it meaning. Attaching the notes to the finding is meant to keep them with the number.

sections.heading: Related sets and waves
sections.text:
When a run holds two or more sets, the app looks for pairs that match once wave, year and version labels are ignored in file names. A strong overlap suggests the same analysis on another wave, and the suggested action is to compare. Sets with a shared label and no files in common may be two parts of one output, and the suggested action is to merge them. You can also compare any two sets directly, choosing which is earlier.
A comparison matches the same model term, or the same segment, in both sets and tests the change against sampling error. For a model term, the difference in log-odds is divided by the combined standard error. For a proportion, the difference in the two estimates is divided by the same kind of combined standard error. Changes beyond about two standard errors are reported as larger than sampling error would explain; the rest are reported as within chance.
Limitation: Two significant results are not a significant change
A term significant in one wave and not in the other has not necessarily changed. The difference between "significant" and "not significant" is not itself statistically significant (Gelman & Stern, 2006). That is why the comparison tests the change itself.
Limitation: Independence and like-for-like
The test assumes the waves are independent samples. If the same people were followed, it will be wrong in either direction. It also assumes the same questions, weights and model specification in both waves. Where the specification changed, a difference in the numbers may be a difference in the model.

sections.heading: Limitations
sections.text:
Limitation: Quality checks use fixed thresholds
Under 30 cases, 80% guide coverage, a design effect of 1.5 and adjusted GVIF cut-offs are conventions. They are sensible defaults, not boundaries in nature, and p values themselves say little about the size or importance of an effect (Wasserstein & Lazar, 2016).
Limitation: Output is classified by shape
Files are sorted from headers, a few rows and the name. An unusual export can land in the wrong kind, which is why the signals are shown and the role can be checked.
Limitation: Reference categories depend on the console
The reference level is read from relevel calls in a pasted console log. Terms for variables whose reference was never set that way are marked as unknown, and the odds ratios still compare with the omitted level.
Limitation: Cluster profiles describe, they do not test
A profile shows how the segments differ on variables that are usually the ones that built them. No test of between-cluster differences is in most output, and the findings say so.
Limitation: Questionnaire wording for model terms is a suggestion
Term group labels such as "Education" are matched to questionnaire items by shared words. Derived measures (scores, segments, recoded variables) have no item and get no match, and every match is worded as something to check.
What this does
- Reads, checks and accepts data files without extra steps, and asks again when the structure changes.
- Attaches and reads a questionnaire or guide, and matches it by code, stem and wording, with every match confirmable.
- Sorts a zip of statistical output into evidence, assurance and context, and shows the signals.
- Checks a set against itself and writes findings that carry their assurance notes.
- Compares two waves of the same output and tests each change against sampling error.
What this does not do
- Decide that data is good enough to use.
- Prove a model is correctly specified or a script correct.
- Re-run any model; it reads the output as given.
- Turn cluster profiles or descriptive tables into tested differences.
- Treat two waves as a panel; the comparison assumes independent samples.

sections.heading: A sensible way to work with it
sections.text:
- Upload the data and, if you have it, the questionnaire or guide beside it. Open the quality panel and read the figures.
- Confirm same-code matches, then look at the wording matches one by one.
- For statistical output, upload the whole folder as a zip with a wave label, and look at the roles and kinds the sorter chose.
- Paste the console log into the set if the script did not export everything. It supplies the reference categories.
- Run Check this set and read every amber marker before you make findings.
- Make findings, then read the assurance notes on each before the finding goes anywhere else.
- For a later wave, upload it as its own set and compare.

pages.title: Preparing your files for import
pages.blurb: How to lay out each kind of file, and what to change in your documents, so the app extracts them accurately

sections.heading: Introduction
sections.text:
Preparing your files for import
How each kind of file is best laid out, and what to change in your documents so the app can read them accurately. Nothing here is compulsory. Files that break these tips are still read, but the more closely a file follows them, the less the reader has to guess, and guesses are where extraction errors come from.
Method guides · about 8 minute read · updated 2026-10-11

sections.heading: Four habits that help every file
sections.text:
- Use the original, not a copy of a copy. A file exported from the source tool (SPSS, Excel, Word, PowerPoint) reads better than a scan or a print-to-PDF of it. Text that a person can select and copy is text the app can read.
- Put each kind of file where it belongs. A Word report uploaded as a table, or a table uploaded as a report, is read by the wrong reader and fails in confusing ways. If something looks wrong straight after upload, check the type first.
- Name files so they can be told apart. A name such as Brand_tracker_W2_2026.sav tells you, and the app, more than final_v3.sav. Wave and year tokens in names are also what lets related sets be matched later.
- Say what is in it, once, near the top. Fieldwork dates, sample size, who was asked, whether figures are weighted. The checks look for these, and a missing base is the most common reason a figure cannot be verified.
Why it works this way
The reader is careful but not clairvoyant. Where a layout is ambiguous it will pick the likeliest reading and flag it. Fixing the ambiguity at source is faster than correcting the flag afterwards.

sections.heading: Reports, decks and briefs
sections.text:
Accepted as PDF, Word or PowerPoint. The app reads the text, pulls out claims, and finds the tables inside the document. The brief and proposal on the objectives page accept PDF, Word, PowerPoint or plain text.
- Send a digital PDF, not a scan. A PDF made from images has no text to read, and table extraction from scans is not supported yet. If all you have is a scan, run it through OCR first, or send the Word or PowerPoint original.
- Prefer the Word or PowerPoint original to a PDF of it. Real tables survive as tables. In a PDF the same table can lose its merged headers.
- Keep tables as tables. A pasted picture of a table is invisible to the reader. Use a real table, with one header row, and avoid merged cells where you can.
- Put the base beside the figure. "42% (n = 512)" can be checked. "42%" cannot. Say whether figures are weighted, and who was asked.
- Make claims findable. One claim per sentence, with the number in the same sentence as the statement it supports, extracts cleanly. A claim that spreads over three sentences, with the figure in a footnote, tends to be extracted without its evidence.
- Use headings that say something. "Satisfaction fell among younger customers" helps more than "Results". Charts need their numbers in labels or a table beside them, because a bar with no values cannot be checked.
- Keep the methodology in the document. Sample, mode, dates, weighting and margin of error in one place give the checks something to test the claims against.
Hard to verify, then easy
Before: "Most customers are now happier with call times (see chart)." After: "Satisfaction with call time rose from 41% to 55% between Wave 1 and Wave 2 (weighted, n = 1 000 each wave; Table 4)." The second version carries its own base, direction, size and source.

sections.heading: Tables that are already summarised
sections.text:
Use the Tables picker for CSV or Excel files that hold counts, percentages or averages, not individual respondents.
- One table per sheet, with the title in the first cell or the sheet name, and the column headers in a single row.
- Answer options down the side, groups across the top. Put the total column first.
- Include a base row (the n for each column). Tables without a stated base cannot be checked for small samples.
- Keep percentages as numbers, with the same decimals throughout. Do not mix counts and percentages in one block without a label.
- Avoid merged cells, notes inside the grid, and blank spacer columns. Move footnotes under the table.
- Say in the title or a note whether the figures are weighted.
Limitation: Percent columns should add to about 100
The checks compare each column with 100 and each count with the total row. A table where they disagree is flagged, and sometimes the cause is rounding, sometimes multiple response, and sometimes an extraction error. A note saying which one saves you a query.

sections.heading: Raw case-level data
sections.text:
Use Raw data for files with one row per respondent: .sav, .dta, .csv or Excel (SAS is excluded pending verification). This is what the cross tab tool works from.
- Prefer SPSS or Stata to CSV. They carry variable labels and value labels, so the tool shows "Very satisfied" and the full question wording instead of codes such as 5 and Q12. A CSV has only what is in its cells, so add a questionnaire if you can.
- One row per respondent, one column per variable. Do not mix tables, titles or totals into the data sheet.
- Give every respondent a unique ID. Duplicated IDs are reported as a quality issue.
- Keep a single header row, with short, unique variable names. Two columns with the same name cause silent confusion.
- Flag missing values properly (system missing, or declared missing codes), and avoid unmarked stand-ins such as 99 or 999. They look like real answers and are the most common cause of strange means.
- Include the weight variable if there is one, and keep it in the same file.
- Multiple response questions work best as one 0/1 column per option, with a shared stem (Q7_1, Q7_2, Q7_3), so they can be grouped.
- Remove variables nobody needs. Very wide files keep only the usable variables, and fewer, cleaner columns make that cut easier to trust.

sections.heading: Transcripts
sections.text:
Use Qual data. The reader splits a transcript into speaker turns, so clear speaker labels matter most.
- Label every turn. Start each turn on a new line with the speaker and a colon: Moderator: , Interviewer: , Thandi: , P3: . Labels like these are picked up as speakers, and Moderator, Interviewer, Facilitator, Researcher, Host and Q are treated as the moderator.
- Be consistent. A label counts only when the same label opens at least two lines, so one spelling per speaker (not Mod, Moderator and Mod. in the same file).
- One interview per file, or clear headings. If one file holds several sessions, separate them with headings such as Interview 1, Respondent 2 or Participant 3 on their own lines.
- Timestamps are welcome. A leading [00:12:40] before the label is accepted and does not stop the speaker being recognised. They also help you find the audio again.
- Unlabelled notes are read as plain paragraphs. That works, but speaker-level counts, moderator share and quiet-member checks then have nothing to measure.
- Mark what you could not hear. Use one consistent marker, such as [inaudible], rather than guessing words. Guessed words get coded as if they were said.
- Keep it as spoken. Do not tidy, summarise or merge turns. Long monologues are split into segments of about 1 200 characters for coding, and quotes are checked back against the original text.
- Remove names and identifying detail before upload, and use codes (P1, P2) if you can.
A transcript layout that reads well
Interview 3[00:00:12] Moderator: Tell me about the last time you called the centre.[00:00:20] P3: It was about my account balance. I waited a long time and then got cut off.[00:00:41] Moderator: What did you do next?

sections.heading: A coding file of your own
sections.text:
If you have already coded the transcripts elsewhere (ATLAS.ti, NVivo, a spreadsheet), the coding can be brought in as Qual data. The app reads three shapes and recounts everything itself, so counts in your file are ignored.
- Theme table. One row per quote, with a column headed Theme or Code and a column headed Quote or Quotation. A Definition column is picked up if present.
- Coded sentences. One row per quote with the codes in another column. Separate several codes in one cell with new lines, semicolons or a vertical bar, not commas, because code names often contain commas.
- Matrix. One row per sentence, one column per code, with 1, x or yes where the code applies.
- Use plain headers on the first row, and give a theme once above its quotes if you merge cells. Merged values are copied down.
- Copy quotes exactly as they appear in the transcript. Quotes that differ from the transcript text may not be placed against it.

sections.heading: Questionnaires and guides
sections.text:
Accepted as PDF or Word, attached to the data file or the transcripts. They are read automatically and matched.
- Print the question code with every question and make it the same as the variable name in the data (Q12, B3a). Same-code matches are the most reliable and can be confirmed in one go.
- Put the question wording, then the answer options, in a consistent order, one option per line.
- Write routing as plain words, next to the question: "ASK IF Q5 = 1 or 2", or "No: GO TO Q10". These are read into rules that separate people who were not asked from people who skipped.
- Send the final fielded version, not a draft. Wording and numbering that changed after programming will not match the data.
- For guides, number the topics and write each as a question or a short prompt. Probes belong under their topic, not as separate topics.
- Choose the right type in the dropdown (survey questionnaire, interview guide or focus group guide), since each is matched differently.

sections.heading: Statistical output
sections.text:
Use Statistical output for model results, cluster profiles, diagnostics and logs. A zip of the whole results folder works best, with a wave label if there is more than one study.
- Send the folder as it came out of the script, so the evidence, the assurance files (diagnostics, validation) and the context (manifest, session info) arrive together.
- Export tables as CSV or Excel, with a header row and named columns (term, estimate, std.error, p.value, conf.low, conf.high). Standard column names are what let the sorter recognise the kind of table.
- Give files descriptive names that say what they are: logit_coefficients.csv, cluster_profile.csv, vif_diagnostics.csv.
- Include the console log or the relevel calls, since the reference category for each factor is read from them.
- Keep Word tables simple. They are read, but plain CSV is the safer choice.
- Name waves consistently (Wave 1, Wave 2, W1, W2). The matching ignores wave and year tokens, so the rest of the name should stay the same between waves.
Limitation: Cross tabs do not belong here
Cross tabulations are built from case-level data inside the app, so that weighting, tests and labels stay consistent. Send the data, not a finished cross tab, when you have the choice.

sections.heading: A short checklist before you upload
sections.text:
- Is each file in the right picker (Reports, Tables, Raw data, Qual data, Statistical output, Questionnaire or guide)?
- Can you select and copy the text in the PDF? If not, find the original.
- Does every table have a header row and a base?
- Does raw data have unique IDs, a weight variable, labelled values and properly marked missing values?
- Does every transcript turn start with a speaker label and a colon?
- Does the questionnaire show the question codes that appear in the data?
- Has the owner cleared the files, with personal information removed or covered?

pages.title: How the research quality review works
pages.blurb: Reviewing a brief or proposal against research practice, how the scores are built, the Overview and its Show filter, Improvements, and where it stops

sections.heading: Introduction
sections.text:
How the research quality review works
How a brief or a proposal is reviewed against good research practice, how its scores are worked out, and how to read the Overview, Improvements and Details. It describes current behaviour and will change as the app does.
Method guides · about 7 minute read · updated 2026-10-22

sections.heading: What the review is for
sections.text: The review rates how well a brief or a proposal is written against a fixed set of research-practice criteria, with a score for each part and what to improve. A proposal can also be compared with its brief. It looks at what the documents say, not at whether the study was then carried out well.

sections.heading: Starting a review
sections.text:
Documents imported as a brief or a proposal are listed in the section with their role. Opening the section makes no model call. Choosing Review brief, Review proposal or Compare shows an estimate first, and nothing runs until you confirm. A comparison is a review of its own and appears in the history of both documents.
The review runs in steps: the documents are read into fixed snapshots, facts are extracted with exact quotes that the app finds in the stored text, and the criteria are then judged over those facts. If steps fail, the review says which, and Retry failed steps runs only those; an interrupted review offers Continue review.

sections.heading: How the scores are built
sections.text:
A model rates each criterion on the release's scale, citing the document. Everything numeric after that is worked out by code from the stored ratings.
Figure | How it is worked out
Criterion | Strong 5, Workable 3, Weak 1, Absent 0. Where a criterion has several observations (one per decision), the lowest counts
Category (proposal) | The average of its rated criteria. A brief's ten dimensions are one criterion each
Overall percentage | Sum of weight times score, over sum of weight times 5, across rated dimensions
Band | Strong at 80% or more, Workable at 60% or more, Weak below
A criterion that is not rated yet, failed, or was dismissed is left out of every average; it is never counted as zero. Absent is a real rating and is counted. With less than half of the total weight rated, no overall figure is given.

sections.heading: The Overview and its Show filter
sections.text:
The Overview shows the overall percentage as a ring and one bar per dimension or category. Clicking a bar or a criterion opens its detail on the right: the criterion's question, the reasons for its rating, the document's own words and what to improve.
The Show filter lists All and each status the review actually has: Strong, Workable, Weak, Absent, then Not rated, Pending and Failed. Choosing one lists only the criteria with that status. A category keeps its heading, bar and score beside its matching criteria, so you can see where each sits, and a category with none is left out.
Why it works this way
The filter narrows the list; it does not rescore. The ring and the category scores stay the figures for the whole review, so a filtered view never reads as a new, better or worse score. Pending, Failed and Not rated are states, not ratings, so they are separate choices and never shown as a band.

sections.heading: Improvements
sections.text: Improvements are grouped by when they can be made: before commissioning or fieldwork, before this decision, and for the next study. Each row shows its criterion with the same bar, score and band as the Overview. Choosing a row opens the improvement on the right first, followed by the criterion's question, the reasons for its rating and the document's own words.

sections.heading: Details, checklists and the export
sections.text:
Details records the reviewer, the source versions, the criteria release, and the model and prompt used. The element checklists say, for each required element of the document type, whether it is present, partial or absent, citing the extracted facts. Points (present 2, partial 1, absent 0) give section and overall percentages over the elements assessed. An element whose status cannot be relied on is marked not assessed and left out; unknown is never scored as absent. The review can be exported as a Word document built from the same view as the screen, with no further model call.
Selection
Opening another review clears the selection and resets the filter to All. A review is shown only while its own document is chosen. Switching between Overview, Improvements and Details keeps the selection. The filter and the selection are not remembered after a reload.

sections.heading: Where it stops
sections.text:
Limitation: Ratings are a model's judgement
The ratings come from a language model working to written criteria. A borderline criterion can land in a neighbouring band on another run. The reasons and quotes are there so you can check and disagree. Scores are a guide to where to look, not a certification.
Limitation: It reviews what is written
A document can describe a sound design that is then carried out badly, or a good study can be written up thinly. The review sees only the text, and only the parts it read: where a document was not read in full, an absence cannot be claimed.
What this does
- Rates a brief, a proposal, or a proposal against its brief, with cited reasons.
- Works out every percentage and band in code from the stored ratings.
- Keeps unrated, pending and failed criteria out of averages instead of counting them as zero.
- Filters the criteria by status without changing any score.
What this does not do
- Run a model when you open the section, or start a review without your confirmation.
- Judge whether the study was done well, only how it is documented.
- Remember the Show filter or selection after a reload.

sections.heading: A sensible way to work with it
sections.text:
- Import the brief and the proposal with their roles, then open Research quality.
- Review the brief first, then the proposal, then compare the two.
- Use Show to go through the Weak and Absent criteria, reading the quotes behind each.
- Work through Improvements in their order: before fieldwork first.
- Retry failed steps before relying on the overall figure.

pages.title: How objectives are framed and checked
pages.blurb: Stated and deduced objectives, filling from a brief or proposal once, reading it again, scoring on four dimensions, checking against insights, and where it stops

sections.heading: Introduction
sections.text:
How objectives are framed and checked
Where a project's research objectives come from, how the app words, scores and tracks them, and how it checks whether the accepted insights answer them. It describes current behaviour and will change as the app does.
Method guides · about 14 minute read · updated 2026-10-22

sections.heading: What an objective is here
sections.text:
An objective is a statement of what the project set out to learn, written as a question or an aim rather than a result. "To determine whether price or service quality drives lapsed-member churn more" is an objective. "Price is the main driver of churn" is a finding wearing an objective's clothes, and the app steers away from that form.
Objectives matter because they are the yardstick for the rest of the work. Findings and insights are discovered without reference to them. Objectives come in at the end, as the test of whether the project delivered what it was commissioned to deliver. Each objective is kept as its own item, so it can be accepted, edited, scored and checked one at a time.
Why it works this way
Discovery stays objective-agnostic on purpose. If findings and insights were steered toward the objectives from the start, anything that did not fit the nearest objective would be forced into it or never surface. The thematic analysis literature warns about exactly this kind of early fitting (Braun & Clarke, 2006). Mapping against objectives once, at the end, lets one insight bear on several objectives, lets one objective need several insights, and lets some insights bear on none.

sections.heading: Where objectives come from
sections.text:
Every objective carries a source, and the source shapes how much the app trusts it.
Tag in the table | Where it comes from | Starting status
Stated | Typed by you at project set-up or added later in the review table, or taken from a brief or proposal you uploaded | Accepted straight away
Inferred | Proposed by the app from the project's findings, when you stated no objective of your own | Accepted automatically
Suggested | Proposed by the app from the findings, when you did already state at least one objective | Pending until you accept it
Provided: typed or read from a brief
At set-up you can type objectives, upload a brief, upload a proposal, or combine them. When a document is supplied, a model reads it and returns two things: the business problem, and the research objectives, numbered if there is more than one. If both a brief and a proposal are given, the proposal is treated as the more considered statement where it is sharper, and the two are reconciled into one set. Anything you typed takes priority over what was extracted: objectives are only taken from the document when the objective box is empty. Each objective added this way shows where it came from ("Added from the proposal ...").
If the document cannot be read, what you typed is still saved, and the form says the fill did not happen, with the reason and a Try the fill again button that chooses the same documents again without overwriting what you typed. A reload still shows the failure until a fill succeeds.
A document is read once. Choosing a brief or proposal that an earlier fill of this project already used (or a copy of it with the same content) makes no new reading and adds nothing; the form says when it was used and how many objectives came from it. This matters because a fresh reading words the same objectives differently, and those would otherwise come back as new ones. An objective read from a document before is not added again even if you have since edited, rejected or deleted it: those are your decisions.
To look for anything new in a document already used, press Read it again for anything new. Lines new to the project are added as suggestions waiting for review, never accepted and never in your stated list, each marked "Suggested on re-reading the proposal ...". In the objectives list, a suggestion that looks like an objective you already have is shown beside it, as a hint only; nothing is merged or hidden. If the objective box is not empty, the lines you typed are added and the document's new lines are not used, and the result names them, so you can clear the box and read again.
The reader is told to write one complete objective per line and never to output a section heading, such as "Secondary objectives:", as a line of its own. A short label from the document (main question, primary, secondary) stays as a prefix with a dash. As a second guard, any line that is a bare heading ending in a colon is dropped when the lines are saved.
The objective box only adds. Lines you save are split into separate objectives, ignoring bullets and numbering, and a line identical to one already saved is not added twice. Editing or removing a saved objective is done one at a time from the list.
Deduced: proposed from the evidence
Once a project has findings, you can ask for suggestions. The app reads up to 120 of the project's findings, grouped by theme, together with the business problem and any objectives you stated, and proposes three to five candidates. Each comes with a short rationale naming the themes that support it. You can ask for more at any time with Suggest objectives from these findings, and from the coverage panel for insights that no objective points at.
Re-running replaces the earlier suggestions that you never touched. Suggestions you edited, objectives you stated and anything you rejected are left alone. The app is also told not to restate an objective that has already been accepted.

sections.heading: How suggested objectives are framed
sections.text:
The model is asked to write each candidate in ordinary research-brief form: "To determine whether...", "To assess the relationship between...", "To understand...". It is told to state what the project sets out to learn and not a conclusion already reached, and to keep the wording of the objective itself free of hedging. The reasoning about which evidence supports it belongs in the rationale.
There is a methodological reason behind this. Proposing a hypothesis after seeing the results, then presenting the same results as a test of it, is a recognised problem (Kerr, 1998). The app works on documents that already exist, so a deduced objective is a reconstruction of the question the evidence appears to address. It is not a hypothesis that the evidence has confirmed. For that reason the model is told to be guided by your own stated objective far more than by the findings list, and the checks below treat deduced objectives differently from stated ones.
Objective or finding?
"To determine whether price sensitivity or service dissatisfaction is the stronger driver of member churn" names the question and leaves the answer open. "Price sensitivity is the main driver of member churn" states an answer, so it would be treated as a claim to verify and not as an objective.

sections.heading: The rules that apply on the way in
sections.text:
Most of the framing guidance lives in the instructions given to the model. The rules enforced in code are fewer and plainer.
- A suggested candidate is kept only if it has both objective text and a rationale. Candidates missing either are dropped. If none survive, nothing is changed and you are asked to try again.
- Suggestions need at least one extracted, generated or coded finding to work from. With none, the request fails with a message saying so.
- Your own starting objective is carried into the list as a candidate in its own right, matched on trimmed text so it never appears twice.
- Suggestions arrive accepted only when you stated no objective. Otherwise they wait as pending, because you have already said what the project is for.
- The project's working objective is rebuilt from the accepted items every time one changes: a single objective as written, several as a numbered list, with stated ones ahead of suggested ones.
Nothing in code tests whether a typed objective is well formed. Wording quality is the job of the scoring step.

sections.heading: Quality scoring: four dimensions
sections.text:
Each accepted objective is scored from 1 to 5 on four dimensions, but only the values 1, 3 and 5 are allowed. There is no 2 or 4, which keeps the scorer from hedging in the middle. The four are added to give a total out of 20.
Dimension | 1 means | 5 means
Specific | A topic or a wish, such as "understand customers" | Names who, which behaviour or attitude, and in what context, so two researchers would read it the same way
Measurable | No observation could tell you it had been answered | Implies a clear measure or comparison, and what result would answer it
Answerable with the data supplied | Nothing the project holds could speak to it | The uploaded documents, findings or variables plainly contain what is needed
Relevant to the decision | No clear link to the decision | Its answer would directly inform or change the decision
A total of 16 or more is rated Strong, 12 to 15 Workable, and below 12 Needs work. Each objective also gets a one-sentence rationale naming the reason for its weakest score and, unless every dimension scored 5, a one-sentence suggestion for rewording it. These appear under the objective as "To sharpen it", and the rationale shows when you hover over the rating.
What "answerable" looks at
This dimension is judged against an inventory the app builds at scoring time: the names and kinds of the uploaded documents, the number of non-rejected findings by origin and type, and up to 60 distinct variable names from imported tables. It lists what exists and says nothing about what it shows, so the score is about coverage and not about results. If nothing has been uploaded, the dimension is scored 3 and the rationale says so. Likewise, relevance is scored 3 when there is neither a decision statement nor a business problem to judge against.
When scoring runs
Scores are tied to the objective's text. An unchanged list is not rescored, an edited one is, and Rescore objectives forces a fresh pass. Scoring also runs after you accept, restore or add an objective. Because the inventory is read at the moment of scoring, rescore after adding data. Objectives are sent to the scorer 20 at a time, up to 200 in one run; any beyond that are left unscored, and Rescore objectives says so. A failure in the automatic run is logged and does not interrupt what you were doing.

sections.heading: Coverage against the insights
sections.text:
Coverage asks whether the project's accepted synthesized insights actually answer each objective and each confirmed decision. It needs at least one accepted insight and at least one objective or decision, and it runs only after synthesis, against the final accepted set.
Status shown | Meaning
Answered | The evidence gives a clear, well-supported answer
Partly answered | Some relevant evidence exists, but it does not fully settle the question or rests on weaker confidence
Gap | No accepted insight bears on this item. The model is told to say so plainly and not to stretch a loosely related insight
Every item gets a short conclusion (capped at 35 words) and a list of the insights that bear on it. The mapping is many to many. A Gap is a verdict the check actually returned. When the check cannot assess every item (the model returned nothing usable, gave two answers for one item, or covered only some of them), nothing is recorded as a Gap: the check fails with a message saying so, the previous results stay as they were, and Check again runs it afresh.
Inferred objectives get no verdict
An objective the app deduced from this project's own evidence cannot fairly be tested against that same evidence, because the test would be circular. In the coverage panel these items are labelled Inferred and show no Answered, Partly answered or Gap status. The same applies to decisions the app proposed. Add an objective of your own if you want a real check.
Evidence without an objective
The panel also lists accepted insights that no stated objective or decision points at. These are real findings the project did not ask about. Because the list is built from stated items only, it appears once at least one stated objective exists and the check has run. If every objective was inferred, the panel says nothing falls outside them, since that would be true by construction. The button beside the list asks the framer for objectives that these insights would answer, and names the insights in the rationale.

sections.heading: The review workflow
sections.text:
Objectives are reviewed in one table, with a row per objective showing its tag, the four scores, the total, the rating and the actions.
Action | What it does
Accept / Unaccept | Puts an objective in or out of play. Only accepted objectives are scored and checked
Edit | Saves your wording and accepts it. A changed text is marked Edited, which protects it from being cleared when suggestions are regenerated. If the objective was changed elsewhere since you opened the editor, nothing is saved: your draft stays and you choose Use the current wording or Replace it with mine
Reject / Restore | Sets an objective aside without deleting it. Restoring returns it to accepted
Delete | Removes it permanently, after a confirmation
Accept all suggested | Accepts every pending suggestion as it stands
Regenerate suggestions | Asks the framer for a fresh set, replacing untouched suggestions only
Remove suggested | Deletes suggestions you have not edited. Stated and edited objectives stay
Score / Rescore | Runs the four-dimension scorer
Check now / Check again | Runs the coverage check
Adding by hand refuses an objective that is already pending or accepted, and names it; one you rejected can be typed in again as a deliberate re-add. Two objectives are the same when their wording matches after ignoring numbering, case, spacing, curly quotes and trailing punctuation; there is no matching by meaning, so a reworded objective is a different one.
Accepting, restoring, adding and regenerating also trigger scoring and a coverage refresh in the background. Rejecting and deleting do not, so after either one the coverage panel may still reflect the earlier list until you press Check again. Likewise, new insights accepted after the last check are not reflected until the check is run again.

sections.heading: The Objectives page
sections.text:
Objectives are set up, scored and checked on one page. Across the top, Objective and context holds the form in three columns: fill in from a brief or proposal, the business problem, and your objectives and audience with Save. Drag the line between two columns to resize them, or use the arrow keys on it; double-click or press Enter on it to make them equal again. Your widths are kept in this browser. The band can be hidden to give the panes below more room.
Below it are three panes. The left lists your stated objectives first, which you can edit or delete there, then any suggestions waiting for review, each with its tag, quality tier and score, and whether the evidence answers it. Selecting one shows it in the middle (its text, Edit, Accept or Unaccept and Delete, four score tiles, the scorer's reasoning and how to sharpen it) with its coverage verdict and linked insights underneath. The right pane holds the coverage check itself and the evidence from the data. With nothing selected, the middle shows every objective in one scored table and the right shows the whole coverage check. Objectives are matched to their results by their wording, not by position, so a re-ordered list does not mismatch a verdict.

sections.heading: Evidence from the data
sections.text:
The right pane also asks the data directly. Each stated objective and confirmed decision is broken into up to three questions, written before any table is seen. Each question is answered with a table built from your case-level data files (SPSS or Stata files, and raw case tables) by the same engine as Cross tabs, and read as supporting, against, mixed, inconclusive or silent. Objectives the app inferred itself are skipped, because testing them against the same data would be circular. It does not read the uploaded reports or any table you already built or imported.
The first time a project has objectives and data but no evidence, it is gathered automatically, once per browser session. The button stays for gathering again. Where an expectation can be measured the stance is computed in code, otherwise a model reads the table and the answer is marked judged. Each answer has a Show table link that opens the table behind it, read-only, and Add to Cross tabs, which moves the table into your draft set so it can be edited and committed into findings. Until you do that, evidence tables stay out of Cross tabs and out of findings, so that findings are not shaped by the objectives.

sections.heading: Where it stops
sections.text:
Limitation: Scores are a model's judgement
The four scores and the coverage statuses come from a language model working to written criteria. A borderline objective can land in a neighbouring band on a second run, and models can misread or overstate (Ji et al., 2023). Treat the score as a prompt to reread the wording, not as a measurement. The rationale is there so you can disagree with it.
Limitation: A strong score is not a good objective
The score judges wording, fit with the uploaded data and link to the decision. It cannot tell whether the objective is the right one for your client, or whether the study design could ever answer it.
Limitation: Answerable depends on what has been uploaded
The inventory lists documents, finding counts and variable names. It does not read the contents, and it caps the variable list at 60. An objective can score well on this dimension because a relevant-sounding variable exists, even when the data behind it is too thin to answer.
Limitation: Deduced objectives are reconstructions
They describe what the evidence looks arranged to address. They are useful for spotting what a report implicitly asked, and they are not a substitute for the question you commissioned. The app does not test them, for the circularity reason given above.
Limitation: Re-read suggestions are matched by words, not meaning
A suggestion is placed beside an existing objective when the two share enough content words. That is a hint for your review: a restatement in different words is not flagged, and nothing is merged. A document deleted since its fill cannot be recognised by its content, so importing it again fills normally.
Limitation: Coverage is only as good as the accepted insights
A Gap may mean the project did not answer the question, or that the relevant insight was rejected, never generated, or not yet synthesized. A model-written conclusion can also overstate how much a loosely related insight settles. Read the linked insights before relying on a status.
Limitation: Checks can go stale
Scores reflect the data at the time of scoring, and coverage reflects the accepted insights at the time of the last check. Neither updates itself after every change.
What this does
- Takes objectives from what you type, from a brief or proposal, or from suggestions drawn from the findings.
- Words suggested objectives as research-brief aims, with a rationale naming the supporting themes.
- Scores each accepted objective on four dimensions and gives a reason and a rewording suggestion.
- Checks each stated objective and decision against the accepted insights and marks it Answered, Partly answered or Gap.
- Lists accepted insights that no stated objective points at.
What this does not do
- Decide whether an objective is the right question for the client.
- Test deduced objectives against the evidence they were deduced from.
- Read the contents of your data when judging whether an objective is answerable.
- Refresh scores and coverage after every change, or guarantee a Gap is a true gap.

sections.heading: A sensible way to work with it
sections.text:
- State your objectives at set-up, or upload the brief or proposal and check the objectives it extracted.
- Add the data, then score the objectives so that the answerable dimension reflects what you hold.
- Reword anything rated Needs work using the suggestion, and read the rationale before accepting it.
- If you stated none, review the suggested objectives critically and edit or reject the ones that are not your question.
- After synthesis, run the coverage check and read the insights behind each status.
- Look at the evidence without an objective, since it is either a missed question or noise.
- Check again after any change to objectives or accepted insights.

sections.text:
