pages.title: How our cross tabulation works
pages.blurb: Weighted tables, bases, rating scales, multiple response, nets, SemanticTabs and StarterTabs, significance, and where they stop

sections.heading: Introduction
sections.text:
How our cross tabulation works
A plain account of how survey data becomes weighted tables in this app, how to read them, how tables become findings, and where the method stops. It is a working document and will grow.
Method guides · about 18 minute read · updated 2026-10-22

sections.heading: What quantitative analysis is
sections.text: Quantitative analysis works with numbers from a structured questionnaire. Everyone is asked the same closed questions, usually with a fixed list of answers, and the results are counted, compared and tested. Done on a well-drawn sample, a percentage can be generalised to a population within a margin of error. That breadth and comparability is its strength. Its limit is depth: it shows how many people do something and how groups differ, and it is much weaker at saying why.

sections.heading: What qualitative analysis is, and how the two fit together
sections.text: Qualitative analysis works with words from interviews and group discussions, read for meaning. It is deep, small-sample and interpretive. Tables tell you what and how much. Transcripts help you understand why. The qualitative guide in this knowledge base covers that side, and the two can be linked: a theme from the interviews can be compared with respondents' answers to a closed question.

sections.heading: What survey data usually looks like
sections.text:
Survey data comes as a file from SPSS (.sav) or Stata (SAS files are not supported yet), or as a CSV or Excel sheet with one row per person. Think of one big grid. Each row is a respondent and each column is a variable, usually one question or one answer option. Large national surveys have thousands of rows and thousands of columns. The app never loads the whole grid into the page. It keeps your file in storage, reads only the list of variables for the picker, and computes each table when you ask for it, from just the columns that table needs.
Four features of survey files matter for everything below.
- Labels. Answers are stored as codes (1, 2, 3) with value labels ("Yes", "No"), and every variable has a question label. The app shows the labels.
- Missing values. A file can flag some codes as missing (refused, not asked). Those are left out of the base. A "Don't know" that is stored as an ordinary answer stays in the table as its own row for a single-choice question, but is left out of averages.
- Weights. Surveys are usually weighted so the sample matches the population (for example by age, sex and province). Each respondent has a weight, and weighted tables count a respondent as many people, not as one.
- Question families. A multiple-response question is stored as several yes/no columns (for example C8_1 to C8_14). A rating battery is stored as one column per item. The app recognises these families from their names and labels and offers them as one unit.

sections.heading: What a cross tabulation is
sections.text:
A cross tabulation (crosstab) splits the answers to one question by the groups of another. The groups go across the top (the banner, or columns), and the answers to the question go down the side (the stub, or rows). Each cell shows how many respondents, or what share, gave that answer in that group.
A small example
Columns: Province (Gauteng, Limpopo, Western Cape). Rows: "Do you own a smartphone?" (Yes, No). The cell for Limpopo and Yes might read 58%, meaning that, weighted, 58% of people in Limpopo said yes.
You can switch each table between three views:
View | What the cell shows | Use it to answer
Column % | Of the people in this column, the share who gave this answer | How do groups differ? (the default, and the one with significance marks)
Row % | Of the people who gave this answer, the share who sit in this column | Who are the people who say this?
Weighted count | The estimated number of people in the population | How many people is that?
Several banner variables can sit side by side in one table (for example province and age group), each as its own block of columns. A variable can have up to 15 groups, and a table up to 60 columns in total.

sections.heading: Weights and bases
sections.text:
Every percentage has a base: the people it is a percentage of. Getting the base right is the most important thing in a table, and most disagreements between two sets of numbers come from different bases. In a weighted table:
- the percentage is the sum of the weights of the people who gave the answer, divided by the sum of the weights of everyone in the base;
- each column shows its unweighted n (how many real respondents), which is the honest guide to how much evidence stands behind it;
- the app also computes an effective base, which is how many equally weighted respondents the weighted sample is worth. It uses the standard approximation (sum of weights) squared, divided by the sum of squared weights. Unequal weights make the effective base smaller than the real count, and it is what the significance test uses.
If you choose no weight the table is unweighted, and it is labelled so when it is saved. The app proposes the survey's person-level or benchmarked weight when it can find one, and variables that only describe the sample design (weights, area codes, identifiers) are never offered as things to measure.
When a base is too small
Cells fall into three tiers by unweighted base. With 30 or more cases a cell is shown normally and can be tested. With 10 to 29 cases the figure is shown in grey italics, and the column header says "indicative only". It is not tested, carries no arrows, and cannot produce a finding. With under 10 a dash replaces the figure, because a percentage of a handful of people is mostly noise and could also point to individuals. If several adjacent columns are thin, group them (for example "Four or more") to get a base large enough to read.

sections.heading: Kinds of questions and how each is tabulated
sections.text:
Kind | How it appears in the data | How the table treats it
Single choice | One column, one answer per person | One row per answer. Column percentages add to 100%. Up to 30 answers; a numeric variable with 25 or fewer distinct values is also treated as categories.
Multiple response | Several yes/no columns, one per option | One row per option. Each option is a percentage of the people who answered that option. A row at the top, "Base: answered this question", shows the people who answered at least one option. Percentages are of people, so they can add to more than 100%.
Rating scale | One numeric column of 10 or more points (0 to 10, 1 to 10), labelled "0" to "10" or with no value labels | One row per answer, with the mean and spread of the codes as well. Don't know and other declared missing codes are left out of the mean. A column the file declares nominal gets no mean.
Rating grid | Several numeric columns without value labels (a 1 to 10 battery) | One row per item showing the average. Codes labelled don't know, refused or not applicable are left out of the average.
Battery | Several labelled, non yes/no columns that share a stem | Each item becomes its own question with its own answers and its own base.
Numeric | One numeric column with many values (age, income) | A single row with the average. Group it into bands first if you want shares.
Why it works this way
For multiple response, the choice of base changes the answer, so it is stated rather than hidden. Each option uses the people who answered that option, and the base row shows the people who answered at least one. This follows standard survey practice: percentages of respondents ("cases") are the right ones for comparing groups, even though they can exceed 100%. Percentages of responses (a share of all mentions) are a different statistic and are not used here.

sections.heading: Nets and grouped categories
sections.text:
A net combines several things into one row so you can read the combination as a unit.
Net of yes/no options
Tick two or more yes/no options in the variable list, name the net (for example "Any government grant") and add it. A person is in the net if they chose at least one of its options, and they are counted once, however many they chose. The base is everyone who answered at least one of those options. Two checks are always true: a net is never smaller than its largest member, and never larger than the sum of its members. If a net is larger than the sum, something is wrong. Adding the members' percentages together would double count anyone who chose several, which is why the app does not do that.
Grouped categories
For a single-choice question, use Group on its chip to combine answer categories. On a row variable, each group is added as a NET row under the categories (for example "Top 2 box"), using everyone with a valid answer as the base, so a net of categories equals the sum of its categories. On a column variable, grouped categories become a single column and the rest stay as they are, which is the usual fix when several columns have too few people ("Three or more SIM cards" instead of three thin columns). A category can sit in only one column group, but may appear in more than one row net.

sections.heading: Significance: what the arrows mean
sections.text:
In the column % view, a green ▲ or a red ▼ marks a cell that differs from the other columns beyond what chance would plausibly produce. The test compares the column with all other people in the same banner variable (the rest of the sample), using a two-proportion test on the effective bases, at the 95% level. For averages it compares the column's mean with the mean of the rest. A column is never compared with the Total column, because the Total already contains it, and that would make differences look more significant than they are. Both groups need an effective base of at least 30 for a test to run.
Three things to keep in mind when you read an arrow.
- It tests chance, not importance. With a large sample, a gap of one or two points can be marked. Look at the size of the gap, not only the arrow.
- Many tests mean some false alarms. At the 95% level, about 1 comparison in 20 is marked even when there is no real difference. A big table has hundreds of cells. By default the app applies a false discovery rate correction across the columns of each banner variable for each row (Bonferroni, or no correction, can be chosen under Table settings), which removes some of those marks. It does not cover the many rows and banners of a workbook (see limitations), so still treat an isolated arrow in a large table with caution, and weigh a repeated pattern more heavily.
- Built-in links can mislead. When the columns and rows are related by construction, the marks are not informative. People with more SIM cards, for instance, will name more networks. Think about whether the pattern is real or mechanical before reporting it.

sections.heading: Ways of making tables
sections.text:
The workspace has five tabs over the same table set: CrossTabs (pick rows and columns, add nets and groups), SemanticTabs (ask in plain English), StarterTabs (a suggested set), ObjectiveTabs(tables built from your research objectives) and All tables. Every table, however it was made, is listed under All tables and goes through the same commit.
SemanticTabs: asking in plain English
You describe a table ("satisfaction by region, women only") and get a setup to check: the rows, the columns, the filters and anything the reader was unsure of. Nothing runs until you press Add table nowor Put this in the workspace. The sentence describing the table is written from the checked setup, not by the model, so it cannot promise something the table does not show.
Asking for a mean or an average of a row adds a mean row above its answers, with the answers kept below. The mean is of the numeric answer codes, weighted with the table's weight, leaving out don't know, refused and not applicable. If the codes may not be an ordered scale (regions, brands), the row says "mean of the answer codes, which may not be in order". A question with text answers, or a set of questions, gets no mean, and the setup says why. Only the mean is offered; other statistics are refused.
SemanticTabs remembers the five newest tables built from the file, and your last three requests in the panel, so you can say "switch the rows and columns of the table just produced" or "the same, but women only". The setup then names the table it starts from. Only that table's variables and filters are taken; nets, combined columns, weight, tests and corrections are set as usual. The tables are remembered after a reload; your requests are not, and Forget my earlier requests clears them.
StarterTabs: a suggested set
StarterTabs proposes columns to split by and builds one draft table for each, with the file's other suitable questions down the side. It recognises demographics first (gender, age, province or region, urban or rural, population group, education, employment), then customer and sample groupings (segment, cohort, tier, customer type, channel, branch and similar), by the words in each variable's name and label. A column needs 2 to 10 answers and at least 90% of people answering. Text answers in a short list ("Segment1", "Yes"/"No") count as categories; free text does not.
Under Columns to split by you can choose the columns yourself, up to four (three in a file of more than 100 variables). The list opens by itself when nothing is recognised. A question rated 0 to 10 or 1 to 10 (10 or 11 distinct numeric values) gets a mean row above its answers. Your choice applies to the open workspace and is not remembered after a reload.

sections.heading: From tables to findings
sections.text:
Nothing is tabulated automatically when you upload a file. A large survey crossed against even a few groups means thousands of tests, and a few will look significant by chance alone, so which comparisons to run is left to you. To get going quickly, the workspace offers an optional starter set: the usual demographic or customer splits (gender, age, province, segment and similar) against the questions in the file, built as drafts (see StarterTabs above). Under about 100 variables it is offered up front and covers up to 40 questions. In larger files it is a smaller, capped suggestion (20 questions). Because a starter set tests so many cells, only differences that survive a false discovery rate correction (Benjamini & Hochberg, 1995) at 5% become findings from it, and those findings say so. "Delete all drafts" clears the set in one click.
Tables are built as a set. Each time you press "Add table to set" the table is added below the previous ones as a draft. Nothing is turned into findings yet, so you can roll tables up, delete any you do not want, and add more. Each table card has a roll up button, a delete button and its own switch between column %, row % and weighted count. Hiding a row or column changes only what you see.
When the set is right, press Commit. The app then writes findings from the committed tables: for each question it takes up to three of the largest marked differences (ranked by the gap between a column and the overall figure), up to 40 findings per table. Each finding states the figures, the base, the effective base, the weight used and the test, and carries caveats that follow the table: how the many comparisons were handled (false discovery rate controlled within the row, and within the table when that check ran; Bonferroni corrected; or uncorrected when no correction was chosen), that the test used the weighted effective base, and whether a survey design was modelled (with a named PSU or strata) or the sample was assumed random. Deleting a table archives the findings that came from it; nothing is destroyed.

sections.heading: Limitations
sections.text:
Limitation: a rating scale is recognised by its values
A column with no value labels counts as a 0 to 10 or 1 to 10 scale when it has 10 or more distinct whole-number codes. A scale on which fewer than 10 values were actually given is read as categories, with no mean; set the variable as continuous to get its average. A count variable with 10 or more values gets a mean too, which is still the mean of the counts. StarterTabs and the grouping words are matched by wording, not meaning: a split named otherwise needs choosing by hand.
Limitation: the sample design is only as good as what you tell the app
If you name a PSU (cluster) variable, and ideally a strata variable, the app uses Taylor series linearised standard errors, the method behind the R survey package. On the FinScope 2024 file, with the strata rebuilt as in the original R run, those standard errors matched R to within 0.3% in every cell tested. Without a design the app uses the Kish effective base, which only reflects unequal weights. On the same file that understated or overstated the design-based error by up to a third, depending on the cell, so treat a weights-only arrow as indicative. Strata that contain a single PSU are pooled, which can only widen intervals. Finite population corrections are not applied.
Limitation: the correction is a choice
Many columns are tested at once, so some differences appear by chance. The default is the Benjamini-Hochberg false discovery rate (Benjamini & Hochberg, 1995), applied across the columns of each banner variable for each row. Bonferroni is stricter and no correction is available. A correction can only remove marks, never add them. The correction does not cover the many rows and banners in a workbook, so a finding should still be read as a lead.
Limitation: the whole-table test is first order
Each question gets a whole-table test against each banner variable, using a first-order Rao-Scott adjustment (Rao & Scott, 1981): the chi-square is divided by an average design effect. It is an approximation, and without a design the effect comes from the weights alone, which is optimistic for a clustered sample.
Limitation: tables describe association, not cause
A difference between groups can reflect something else that differs between them (age, income, access). A table cannot separate those explanations. Findings describe differences, not reasons.
Limitation: a base reflects who was asked, which the file may not say
The app can tell who answered a question. It cannot always tell who was supposed to be asked. A missing answer might mean a refusal, or that the question was skipped by routing. If the file does not mark the difference, a base can be smaller or larger than the intended universe. Check the questionnaire for routing on any question where the base looks odd.
Limitation: grouping is your decision
Net and group definitions are analyst choices. Combining categories changes the result, and the same categories can be grouped in different defensible ways. State the grouping when you report a net.
Limitation: small groups hide real differences, and show false ones
With few people in a column the test has little power, so real differences go unmarked, and figures on bases under 30 are indicative only (under 10 are hidden). Combine thin categories before concluding that groups do not differ.
What this does
- Weights each cell, states the base, and shows unweighted, weighted and effective bases.
- Keeps every option of a multiple-response question, each on the correct base.
- Builds nets and grouped categories from respondent-level data, never by adding percentages.
- Offers an optional starter set split by demographics, customer groupings or columns you choose, with false discovery rate control on the findings it yields.
- Turns a plain-English request into a setup you check first, including a requested mean, and follows a reference to a table you built earlier.
- Tests each column against the rest of its banner variable (Taylor series variance when a design is given), shows column-pair letters, a whole-table test, a correction setting and an Excel export, marks bases under 30 as indicative only, and hides figures under 10.
- Keeps tables as drafts until you commit, and archives findings if a table is deleted.
What this does not do
- Know your sampling design unless you name the PSU and strata variables.
- Correct for the many tables and banners across a whole workbook.
- Replace a statistician's review of a complex-sample analysis.
- Tell you why two groups differ.

sections.heading: A sensible way to work with it
sections.text:
- Open the workspace and choose the banner: the groups you care about, such as province or age band.
- Check the weight proposed. Use it unless you have a reason not to.
- Add the questions to measure. Add a whole family at once, or tick yes/no options to build a net.
- Look at the bases first, then the percentages, then the marks. Group thin categories where needed.
- Delete tables that only show a mechanical relationship, and add the cuts that answer your questions.
- Commit the set, then review the findings and caveats before using any of them in a report.

sections.text:

pages.title: How our qualitative analysis works
pages.blurb: From transcripts to codes and themes, what the numbers mean, and where they stop

sections.heading: Introduction
sections.text:
How our qualitative analysis works
A plain account of how a transcript becomes codes, themes and findings in this app, what each number means, and where the method stops. It is a working document and will grow.
Method guides · about 14 minute read · updated 2026-10-08

sections.heading: What qualitative analysis is
sections.text:
Qualitative analysis works with words, not counts. People are asked open questions in an interview or a group discussion, and what they say is read for meaning: what matters to them, how they explain their choices, what worries them, and what they take for granted. Its strength is depth. It can show why people behave as they do and surface ideas nobody thought to ask about. Its weakness is the flip side of that strength: the samples are small, they are rarely chosen at random, and the reading involves judgement.
In this app the method is closest to codebook thematic analysis (Braun & Clarke, 2006), with some of the counting habits of qualitative content analysis. A code is a short label for an idea that recurs. A theme is a broader pattern of meaning that several codes are facets of. The app is called "content analysis" in everyday talk, and that is fine, but it helps to know that the reading is interpretive and that the counts describe the sample you have, not a wider population.

sections.heading: What quantitative analysis is, and how the two fit together
sections.text:
Quantitative analysis works with numbers from a structured questionnaire: everyone answers the same closed questions, usually with a fixed set of answer options, and the results are counted, compared and tested. Its strength is breadth and comparability. With a well-drawn sample, a percentage can be generalised to a population, within a margin of error. Its weakness is shallowness: it can tell you that 40% of people use a mobile wallet, but not why the other 60% do not.
The two work best together. Quantitative results tell you what is happening and how much. Qualitative results help explain why. The cross tabulation guide in this knowledge base covers the numbers side. This guide covers the words side, and the app can link the two (see the checks below).

sections.heading: What the data usually looks like
sections.text:
The raw material is a transcript: a verbatim record of an interview or a focus group, usually typed from an audio recording. It is a sequence of turns, each one a speaker saying something. A typical fragment:
A transcript fragment
Moderator: How do you usually pay your electricity?
Thandi: I buy prepaid at the shop, because I never know what the bill will be. With the app I get scared I will overspend.
Sipho: Same for me. I trust the shop. I can see the slip.
Three features of this kind of data shape everything that follows.
- Moderator turns are context, participant turns are evidence. What the moderator says shapes the answer but is not a finding. Themes are drawn only from what participants said.
- Short replies lean on the question before them. "Same for me" only means something because of what came just before. The app shows the preceding question when it codes such a turn.
- Respondents come with attributes. A respondent may be linked to a profile (province, age group, customer type) and, where you have the survey data, to their answers to closed questions.

sections.heading: How the app reads a transcript
sections.text: Before any coding, the transcript is split into turns. The app recognises speaker labels such as "Moderator:" or a name followed by a colon, timestamps, and headings such as "Interview 3". Labels like Moderator, Interviewer, Facilitator or Q are treated as the moderator; the rest are participants. Very long turns are cut at sentence boundaries so every piece is still a verbatim stretch of the original. If the automatic reading is wrong, you can re-read the same transcript with a different reading (labels, headings, paragraphs, or none) and choose which speakers are moderators. That replaces the turns, which clears anything tied to the old turns (calibration samples, negative cases, respondent links), so it is best done before the detailed checks.

sections.heading: How codes and themes are created
sections.text:
This is the core of the method. It runs in four steps, plus a grouping step, and every step leaves a record. A language model does the reading at each step, and a researcher can inspect and change the result.
Step 1: open coding, three independent times
The model reads the transcript the way a qualitative researcher would on a first pass. It notes recurring ideas, reactions and concerns, and proposes a small number of themes (roughly four to eight), each with a short name, a one or two sentence statement of what the transcript shows, and one representative quote. The quote must be a participant's words, copied exactly, from within a single turn.
This pass is run three times, independently. A single pass can name different themes from a second pass over the same text, and one run cannot show that. Three runs is the smallest number that shows whether a theme is stable (found in all three, in some, or in only one). It also triples the cost of this step. For very long transcripts each run is shown the first 60,000 characters, cut at a turn boundary, and the cut is recorded. The codebook is still applied to the whole transcript in step 3.
Quote check. Each theme's quote is looked up in the participant turns. A theme whose quote is not really in the transcript is dropped before anything is merged. This is why every quote you see in a finding is verbatim by construction.
Step 2: consolidation into a codebook
The themes from the three runs are merged into one codebook: ideas that appear in several runs under different names become one code, and genuinely different ideas stay separate. The model may not add an idea that no run found. A codebook holds at most 12 codes. Each code has:
- a short name (two to five words);
- a definition that stands alone, so someone who has not seen the transcript could decide whether a remark belongs;
- an inclusion rule (when to code a remark here);
- an exclusion rule (what looks similar but does not belong, naming the nearest other code).
The app also records how many of the three runs found each code. That count is computed from the merge, not asserted by the model, and it is shown as "found in 2 of 3 runs".
Step 3: applying the codebook to every participant turn
The codebook is now applied to every participant turn of the whole transcript, not only the part the open runs saw. For each turn the model lists the codes it clearly expresses. A turn can carry more than one code, or none. It judges only what the participant said in that turn, a short reply is coded only if the preceding question makes its meaning clear, and an exclusion rule always wins over an inclusion rule. The codebook is versioned. If you edit it (rename a code, tighten a definition, merge two codes), the edit becomes a new version, the old one is kept, and the codebook is applied again to the stored turns.
Step 4: findings
Each code that is applied to at least two turns becomes a finding, tagged as coded. Its quote is taken from a turn the code was actually applied to. A code seen in only one turn is kept in the codebook but does not become a finding, because one remark is an anecdote, not a pattern.
Grouping codes into themes
A flat list of codes is not yet an analysis. Following Braun and Clarke's phase of generating themes, the app groups related codes under broader themes, so the result is a tree: Theme > code. The rules are deliberate. Use between two and seven themes. Every theme holds at least two codes. A code belongs to at most one theme. A code that fits nowhere is left out and stands as a theme of its own. And a theme is a shared idea, not a topic heading, so it is named as a short noun phrase such as "Cost of unreliable connectivity" rather than "Connectivity". The app also offers a second look that merges themes that overlap. You can edit the grouping in the codebook panel, or ask for it to be redone.
Across several transcripts
When a study has two or more coded transcripts, the app can group the codes of all of them under main themes that hold across the study. It needs at least two coded transcripts and at least four codes. Each code keeps its link to its own transcript, so a main theme can always be traced back to who said what.
Coding you did yourself
If you coded a transcript elsewhere (ATLAS.ti, NVivo, Dedoose or a spreadsheet), you can import it. No model does the coding: each quote in your file is looked up in the transcript, the turn it sits in gets your code, and your codes become the codebook (up to 40 per transcript). From there the counts, quotes and findings are built the same way as for model-coded transcripts. Counts in your file are never trusted; they are recounted from the transcript.
Why it works this way
The app does not ask the model to simply summarise. It asks it to code against explicit definitions, then counts what was coded, and every quote can be checked against the source. The purpose is that a researcher can disagree with a code, edit it, and see exactly what changes, which a free-form summary would not allow. Every model call is logged with a fingerprint of its instructions and its input, so a coding run can be audited later.

sections.heading: What the codes, themes and numbers mean
sections.text:
Term | What it is | How to read it
Turn | One speaker saying something, in the order spoken | The unit that gets coded. A turn can carry several codes or none.
Code | A named idea with a definition and inclusion and exclusion rules | A label for a recurring idea. It is a tool for reading, not a fact about the world.
Theme | A pattern of meaning that several codes are facets of | A claim about what the codes add up to. It is an interpretation and should be read as one.
Turns coded | How many participant turns carry the code | Volume of talk. One talkative person can inflate this.
Respondents | How many different people voiced the code, out of how many in the study | Spread across people. Usually the better guide to how widespread an idea is.
Found in n of 3 runs | How many of the three independent open-coding passes found the idea | Stability of the code. Found in 3 of 3 is steadier than 1 of 3, which deserves a closer look.
Counts are always shown with their base, for example "7 of 12 respondents". A number without its base is not interpretable. These counts describe this sample. They are not percentages of a population, and the app deliberately does not run significance tests on them.

sections.heading: The checks that sit on top
sections.text:
Coding by a model is a proposal, and the app gives you ways to test it. None of these is a pass or fail gate. They are evidence to weigh.
Check | What it does | How to read it
Agreement with your own coding | You judge a sample of turns yourself. The app compares your judgement with the model's, code by code, using Cohen's kappa (agreement beyond chance). | Bands follow Landis and Koch (1977): up to 0.20 slight, 0.21 to 0.40 fair, 0.41 to 0.60 moderate, 0.61 to 0.80 substantial, above 0.80 almost perfect. Below 20 judged turns, or with very few positives, the app warns that kappa is unstable.
Random audit | An alternative to the targeted sample. Turns are drawn at random within groups (turns with no theme, and turns grouped by their rarest theme), you code them blind, and the app estimates how often the model's themes match yours exactly across the whole transcript, with a range. | Because the draw is random, this is the only check that speaks for the transcript as a whole. The suggested size is about 15% of participant turns, between 30 and 120, in line with the 10 to 25% of units that O'Connor and Joffe (2020) suggest double coding. The per-theme rows rest on few turns each. A wide range means judge more turns.
Fuller agreement per theme | Beside kappa, the app shows agreement on the turns where either of you applied the theme, raw agreement, and a note when a theme is rare or very common. | Kappa falls when a theme is rare or very common even if two coders almost always agree (Byrt et al., 1993), so read it with the other figures and not alone.
Stability check | The app applies the same codebook to the same turns again, once or more, and shows which turns came out differently. Those turns go to a queue for you to settle. | Turns the model codes differently from run to run are where it is least reliable; in one study, annotations that were perfectly consistent across repeats were more accurate (Pangakis & Wolken, 2024). It flags where to look. It does not show that a stable turn is right, because repeated runs share blind spots.
Settling flagged turns | For each flagged turn you first tick the themes you think apply, before the model's themes or the other runs are shown. That first answer is locked. Then the model's side appears and you settle the turn. | Seeing a suggestion first pulls people towards it, so the first judgement is yours. The app also tracks how often you change the model's coding and how fast you decide, and shows a prompt if nearly everything is accepted quickly. It is a prompt, not a verdict.
Negative cases | The app searches for passages that cut against a code, up to three per code, and shows them with the quote. | A pattern that survives its counter-examples is stronger. Read them, then decide whether to tighten the code.
Data quality | Words per respondent, how much the moderator talks, how dominant the most talkative speakers are, duplicate turns, how much of the transcript was coded. | Respondents with under 50 words are flagged as thin. A moderator who talks a lot, or one speaker who dominates, changes what the themes represent.
Saturation | Code saturation: after each added respondent, did new codes still appear? Meaning saturation: did later respondents add a new dimension within a theme, shown with a verbatim excerpt? | Evidence about whether the sample was big enough, not proof (Guest et al., 2006; Hennink et al., 2017). It is a prompt to read, not a verdict.
Focus group echoes | In a group, a turn that echoes another speaker's coded turn is flagged. | Agreement in a group is not always independent agreement. Echoes are counted separately so they do not look like extra evidence.
Link to survey answers | The model proposes which closed survey questions a theme should relate to. Respondents who voiced a theme but answered on the unexpected side of the median are flagged. | A flag is a prompt to reread the transcript. It could mean a say-do gap, a misread question or a wrong code. It is not a finding.
Themes by respondent attribute | Which themes go with which respondent groups, and which themes appear together. | Counts only, with their base. Groups with fewer than 5 respondents are flagged as small. No significance tests, because with interview-sized samples a p-value would imply more certainty than the data can carry.

sections.heading: Limitations
sections.text:
Every method has edges. These are the ones that matter most here, stated so you can judge how far to rely on a result.
Limitation: a model does the first reading
The codes are proposed by a language model, which can misread irony, local expressions, code-switching or a short reply that depends on context. It can also miss an idea or over-split one. That is why the codebook is editable, quotes are verified, and agreement checks exist. Treat the first codebook as a draft.
Limitation: runs are not identical
Running the same transcript again can produce somewhat different codes. The three-run design makes this visible, as the "found in n of 3 runs" count, but it does not remove it. Once you have edited and accepted a codebook, that version is what is applied, and it is stable.
Limitation: themes are interpretations
A theme is a researcher's (here, partly a model's) account of what the codes mean together. Two careful analysts can group the same codes differently. Reflexive approaches treat this as a feature of the method, not a flaw to remove (Braun & Clarke, 2019), which is why the grouping is editable rather than final.
Limitation: small, non-random samples
Interview and focus group samples are usually small and purposively chosen. Counts describe who you spoke to. They cannot be read as how common an idea is in the population, and a theme voiced by two of twelve people may still be important.
Limitation: long transcripts are only partly seen in the open pass
Each open coding run reads up to the first 60,000 characters. A theme that appears only late in a very long transcript may not make it into the draft codebook, although the codebook is applied to the whole text once it exists. Check the data quality panel for a recorded cut.
Limitation: a turn is a coarse unit
Coding works at the level of a whole turn. A long turn can contain several ideas, and a code applied to it marks the turn, not the exact sentence. Turns over 1,200 characters are split, which helps, but the unit is still approximate.
Limitation: the sample can be dominated by a few voices
Turns coded counts talk, not people. In a focus group one confident speaker can account for most of a theme. Use the respondent counts and the echo and speaker-share checks alongside the turn counts.
Limitation: agreement statistics depend on small numbers
Kappa can swing sharply when it rests on few judged turns or on a code that is rarely applied. The app says so when that is the case. A moderate kappa on a rare code is not a reason to discard it, and a high kappa on a trivial code is not a reason to trust it.
Limitation: the audit is one researcher's reading
The audit and the settled turns compare the model with you. You are one reader, not a gold standard, and a low match can mean a vague definition as easily as a poor model call. Until an audit has been drawn and judged, the app labels the themes as not yet audited.
Limitation: no claim of causation or representativeness
A theme such as "price sensitivity" says people talked about price in a certain way. It does not show that price caused anything. Findings are written as what participants said and did, not why events happened across a market.
What this does
- Reads transcripts turn by turn and keeps moderator turns as context only.
- Builds a versioned codebook with definitions, inclusion and exclusion rules.
- Checks every quote against the source and counts codes from the transcript.
- Lets you edit, re-apply, import your own coding, and test the model against your judgement.
What this does not do
- Replace a researcher's judgement about what a theme means.
- Tell you how common an idea is in a population.
- Run significance tests on interview-sized counts.
- Guarantee identical codes on every rerun before a codebook is accepted.

sections.heading: A sensible way to work with it
sections.text:
- Check that the transcript was read correctly (speakers, moderator turns) before anything else.
- Run the coding, then read the draft codebook as a researcher would. Rename, merge or tighten codes.
- Draw a random audit and judge it. Read the overall match and the agreement per code, and fix definitions where agreement is poor.
- Run the stability check and settle the flagged turns, coding each one yourself before looking at the model.
- Read the negative cases and the thin respondents. Decide what each means for the claim.
- Group codes into themes and edit the grouping until the themes say something you would defend.
- Report themes with the number of respondents and the quote, and state the sample and its limits.

pages.title: How reports are built
pages.blurb: How the Insights Report is built from reviewed evidence only, the Word report and slide deck layouts, the SCQA story narrative, caveats, exports, and where they stop

sections.heading: Introduction
sections.text:
How reports are built
How the Insights Report is assembled from reviewed evidence, what the Word report and the slide deck each contain, how the story narrative is structured, how caveats travel with the content, and what the exports cannot do. It describes current behaviour and will change as the app does.
Method guides · about 9 minute read · updated 2026-10-08

sections.heading: What the report outputs are
sections.text:
A report in this app is not written from scratch at the end. It is a layout of material that has already been extracted, verified, synthesised and reviewed, plus a thin layer of narrative framing that ties it together. Almost everything a reader sees on a page was a finding, an insight or a recommendation first, and was accepted by a person before it got there.
That design has a practical consequence. If a report reads wrongly, the fix is rarely in the report. It is usually upstream: a finding that should have been rejected, an insight that was accepted too early, or an objective that was never recorded. The report shows what the earlier stages hold, no more and no less.
Why it works this way
Reports are where evidence meets an audience, and that is where a stray number or a dropped caveat does the most harm. Keeping the report a view onto reviewed material, instead of a fresh piece of authorship, is what stops the final document from drifting away from the checked evidence beneath it.

sections.heading: The three report types
sections.text:
The Insights Report section of a project produces two client-facing documents from one underlying narrative. A third element, the discovery report, is a section that appears inside both.
Type | What it is | Built for
Slide deck (.pptx) | A persuasive argument in the Situation, Complication, Question, Answer shape, led by a governing thought, then supported by pillars of insights | Presenting to a room, where the answer should come first
Word report (.docx) | A conventional research report: executive summary, introduction, methodology, findings, insights, recommendations, next steps | Reading at your own pace, and being quoted from or circulated
Discovery report (a section) | A separate section that lists what the analysis added beyond the original report, and where it contradicts it | Telling a reader which content was checked and which was originated here
Both documents read from the same stored narrative, so there is one thing to regenerate. Regenerating updates what both exports will produce next. Neither export keeps its own copy of the story.
Separate from the Insights Report, the app also offers narrower exports: decks of findings, insights or recommendations, an Excel workbook of findings, and a CSV of removed findings. They are listed under export formats below.

sections.heading: Only reviewed evidence goes in
sections.text:
The Insights Report will not generate until at least one synthesised insight has been accepted. It is built on the synthesised layer, not the individual pre-insights, so a run with dozens of pre-insights behind a few accepted synthesised ones tells a story with a handful of proof points, not dozens.
Content | What qualifies it | Where it appears
Insights | Synthesised insights marked accepted | Narrative pillars, insight cards, insight sections
Recommendations | Accepted, and anchored to a synthesised insight | Recommendation cards and the Recommendations section
Findings | Accepted, with a verdict of robust or use with caution | The Findings section of the Word report, and chart pages
Objectives and decisions | Those the objective and decision check has run against | Objectives and decisions pages, and the Word report section that mirrors them
Findings rated not supported or insufficient information are left out of the report. Rejected material and anything still awaiting review is left out too. This is deliberately stricter than the working views in the app, where you can see everything. A document that goes to a client uses the conservative bar.
The model does not retype the evidence. In the narrative step it points at insights by number, and the code turns those numbers into stored ids. When a slide or section shows an insight, its headline, observation and implication are pulled straight from the saved record. What a researcher reviewed is therefore what appears, word for word.

sections.heading: How the story narrative is built
sections.text:
One model call reads the accepted insights, the accepted recommendations and the project context (business problem, research objective, decision statement, audience) and proposes how they add up. The structure it is asked to follow is the Pyramid Principle in its Situation, Complication, Question, Answer form: lead with the answer, then show the supporting arguments beneath it.
Part | What it does | Length held in code
Executive summary | Two to four sentences a senior reader could stop after: the answer and the top action | 115 words
Situation | The context the decision sits in | 75 words
Complication | The tension that makes it matter now | 75 words
Question | The decision the project exists to inform. Falls back to the recorded decision statement | No cap
Governing thought | The one-sentence answer the rest of the story supports | 34 words
Pillars | Two to five supporting arguments, each with a full-sentence headline and a one-sentence so what | 22 words and 30 words
Caveats | Two to four limits grounded in the specific evidence, not generic disclaimers | 38 words each
Recommendations intro | One sentence leading from evidence into action | 32 words
What the code, not the model, controls
- Which insights sit under which pillar. The model proposes groupings. Code discards invalid numbers, de-duplicates, and keeps at most three insights per pillar, ranked by confidence tier (strong first) and then by quality score. The number left out is stored, so the deck can say there are more.
- Length. Every field is cut to its word limit after the model has answered, in case the model overruns.
- Retries and fallback. If no usable pillar comes back, the call is repeated up to three times. If it still fails, the report falls back to one pillar per accepted insight, using that insight's own headline and implication. That is a worse story but a true one.
The model is also told to write the framing in plain business English and to keep p-values, odds ratios and similar notation out of the narrative fields. That is an instruction, not a check. The statistical detail stays with the evidence underneath.
Reading a pillar
A pillar headline might read "Informal traders save in short bursts, not on a schedule". The model wrote that sentence. The two or three insight cards beneath it were written earlier, reviewed by you, and are shown exactly as stored. If the headline claims more than the cards support, the cards are the better guide.

sections.heading: The Word report, section by section
sections.text:
The Word report follows the order a research report trains readers to expect. It is deliberately not the deck's answer-first shape, because a reader working through pages does not need to be persuaded in the same way as a room.
- Title block with the key question, the audience if recorded, and the date generated.
- Executive summary.
- Introduction: business problem, research objective, background (situation and complication) and the key question.
- Methodology: the original study's method as stated in the uploaded material, then a list of source documents grouped by kind.
- Findings, grouped by theme, each with its verdict label, and a chart for themes that qualify.
- Insights: the governing thought, then each theme with its insights, then how the objectives and decisions were answered.
- New insights beyond the report (when there is anything to say).
- Recommendations, each with priority, owner role, timeline and success metric.
- Next steps: gaps worth following up, scope and limitations, and a plain note on how the report was produced.
The methodology section needs a word of care. It describes how the underlying research was done, and only what the uploaded brief, proposal or report actually says. If none of it states a method, the section says so instead of inferring one. How this app processed the material is kept in a separate note near the end, so the two are not mistaken for each other.
Charts in the Findings section are drawn on the server from the same findings that appear as text. A theme gets a chart only when all of its findings are computed table comparisons. A theme that mixes in claims taken from a report stays text only.

sections.heading: The slide deck, slide by slide
sections.text:
The deck is built to persuade, so it states the answer early and then spends its remaining slides proving it. The sequence below is the general order. Some parts appear only when there is content for them.
Slides | Content | Appears when
Title and roadmap | Project title, the key question, audience, and a map of the deck's own sections | Always
Executive summary | The opening paragraph | A summary was generated
SCQA overview, Situation, Complication | The argument at a glance, then each build-up step on its own slide | Always
Governing thought | The answer as a pull-quote, with the question beneath | Always
Objectives and decisions | Each objective or decision with a status badge: resolved, partial, gap or inferred. A slide names any accepted insights that none of them asked about | The objective and decision check has run
Evidence charts | One chart per qualifying theme | A theme has chart-eligible findings
New beyond the report | Net-new insights and findings, and contradictions | There is something to show
Argument map and pillars | A map of the pillars, then each pillar with its headline, so what and insight cards | Pillars exist
Recommendations | Action cards with a priority badge, owner, timeline and metric, preceded by a divider | Always, paged
Caveats and scope | The narrative caveats and a footnote on what the content is based on | Caveats exist
Text on slides is shrunk in steps to fit its box and, as a last resort, cut with an ellipsis. Long headlines and long insight text are therefore the most likely to be shortened on a slide. The full wording is always in the app and in the Word report.

sections.heading: What the analysis added beyond the report
sections.text:
When a project starts from an existing report, two kinds of content end up side by side: claims the report made and the app checked, and things the analysis surfaced that the report never said. A reader is entitled to know which is which. The discovery section separates them.
- New insights. Accepted synthesised insights, each with a provenance line. The line says, for example, that the insight combines several claims the report made into something none of them said alone, or that it is built entirely from new findings the report did not contain.
- New findings from the data. Accepted findings computed from the supplied tables, rated robust or use with caution, that no report claim points at. A list of up to twelve is shown, strongest first, with a count of how many more passed verification and sit in the Findings section.
- Where the evidence contradicts the report. Each claim the report made that was rated not supported because of a new finding, a new insight, or another claim in the same report, quoted next to what contradicts it and the reason.
- How far this could be checked. If the project had only a report and no underlying data, a note says statistical verification could not run, and that every verdict should be read with that in mind.
If there is nothing to say and nothing to warn about, the section does not appear. The aim is to avoid a hollow heading that suggests a check that did not happen.

sections.heading: How caveats are carried through
sections.text:
A caveat that lives only in the app is easy to lose when the content moves into a document. The report tries to keep the important ones attached in several places.
Caveat | Where it shows up
Verdict tier on a finding | Written beside each finding in the Word report and the new findings list: robust or usable with caution
Confidence tier on an insight | A badge on each insight card in the deck. It pairs a symbol with a text label, so it still reads on a black and white printout
Quality tier on a new insight | Labelled qualified, partial or finding level in the discovery section
Thin or exploratory evidence | The narrative caveats, which are asked to name which tier is thinnest and where a pillar rests on exploratory support
Inferred objectives | A note explaining that objectives generated from the project's own evidence cannot show the research answered what was asked, so no verdict is given
Gaps | Listed under next steps as places where the accepted evidence did not resolve an objective or decision. A gap is named, not hidden
Report-only input | The verification note in the discovery section
Scope footnote | States that the content rests only on what was accepted as of the generation date, and that confidence reflects how well triangulated an insight is, not how important it is
One distinction is easy to miss. Confidence and importance are separate. A well triangulated insight can be minor, and an exploratory one can matter a great deal. The report labels the first and leaves the second to you.

sections.heading: Export formats
sections.text:
Export | Format | Contents
Insights Report deck | .pptx, 16:9 widescreen | The full story deck described above
Insights Report | .docx | The full Word report described above
Findings deck | .pptx | One slide per theme. Accepted findings only by default, or all findings with each one tagged by its review status
Findings workbook | .xlsx | Every finding as a row, for filtering and pivoting in Excel. Accepted only or all
Removed findings history | .csv | The audit trail of findings removed or replaced, for answering why a number changed between drafts
Insights and recommendations also have their own decks, with an accepted-only or all choice. Exports are built fresh each time you click, from whatever was generated or accepted most recently. The two Insights Report files are named from the project name with a report suffix.

sections.heading: Limitations
sections.text:
Limitation: The framing is model-written
The executive summary, situation, complication, governing thought, pillar headlines and caveats are authored by a model. Models can overstate, soften or slightly reword what they summarise (Ji et al., 2023). The insight cards beneath are verbatim, so check the framing against them before you present it.
Limitation: A snapshot, not a live view
The narrative is stored when you generate it. If you accept, reject or edit insights afterwards, the framing does not change until you regenerate. Recommendations are read at export time, so the two can drift apart. Regenerate after any meaningful change in review decisions.
Limitation: Highlight reel, not an audit trail
The deck shows at most three insights per pillar and drops findings that were not rated robust or usable with caution. Everything remains reviewable in the app, but a reader of the document alone will not see all of it.
Limitation: Verdicts do not travel as proof
A finding labelled robust in the report means the evidence in the material supported it as worded. It does not mean the claim is true of the world, and significance is a narrow statement that is easily over-read (Wasserstein & Lazar, 2016). Table findings are corrected for many comparisons within their own table (by default the false discovery rate; Benjamini & Hochberg, 1995), not across the tables of a project, and a contrast between two results is not itself tested (Gelman & Stern, 2006).
Limitation: Gaps depend on what was recorded
The objectives and decisions pages exist only if the check has run, which needs objectives or decisions to have been recorded. A project with neither skips straight to the pillars, and the report will not point out what it was never told to look for.
Limitation: Fixed layout, no custom branding
The deck uses a brand-neutral palette and fixed layouts. Text that does not fit is shrunk or truncated. The Word report is plain by design. There is no template, logo or style option, and there is no PDF export. If you need one, print or convert the Word file yourself.
Limitation: Charts are limited to computed comparisons
Only themes made entirely of table-computed findings get a chart. Evidence quoted from a report is shown as text, even when it contains numbers.
What this does
- Builds a deck and a Word report from one stored narrative, using only accepted material.
- Shows insight text exactly as reviewed, with confidence and verdict labels attached.
- Separates what the original report said from what the analysis added, and flags contradictions.
- Names gaps against recorded objectives and decisions, and carries narrative caveats and a scope note.
- Exports to .pptx and .docx, with findings available as .pptx, .xlsx and removed-findings history as .csv.
What this does not do
- Check the model-written framing against the evidence for you.
- Refresh the narrative automatically when review decisions change.
- Show every accepted insight or every finding in the deck.
- Judge which insights matter most. It ranks by confidence and quality, not by importance.
- Offer PDF export, custom templates or client branding.

sections.heading: A sensible way to work with it
sections.text:
- Finish reviewing findings, insights and recommendations first. Reject what is wrong before you generate.
- Record the business problem, objective and decision statement, since the framing and the objectives pages depend on them.
- Generate the Insights Report and read the executive summary, governing thought and caveats against the insight cards.
- Read the discovery section, particularly any contradictions and the verification note.
- Export the Word report and the deck, and read the Word version for the full picture before presenting the deck.
- If you change any review decision afterwards, regenerate and export again.

pages.title: How findings are produced and checked
pages.blurb: Atomic claims, where they come from, the four verdicts, caveat tags, and where they stop

sections.heading: Introduction
sections.text:
How findings are produced and checked
What a finding is in this app, where findings come from, how they are verified, and what the verdicts and caveat tags do and do not tell you. It describes current behaviour and will change as the app does.
Method guides · about 10 minute read · updated 2026-10-08

sections.heading: What a finding is
sections.text:
A finding is one claim, kept small on purpose, with a link back to the place it came from. "43% of Limpopo adults use mobile money" is a finding. "Mobile money is growing and people trust it" is two or three findings stuck together, and it is much harder to check. Keeping each claim atomic means each one can be verified, accepted or rejected on its own, and later combined with others without carrying hidden baggage.
Findings sit between raw material (documents, tables, transcripts) and insights. They are deliberately descriptive. A finding says what the material says. Why it matters, and what to do about it, comes later and is the job of the insights stage.
Why it works this way
The line between a finding and an insight is the most useful distinction in the whole app. A finding can be true and still not be interesting. An insight has to be both supported and worth acting on. Mixing the two is how reports end up with "insights" that are really just restated numbers.

sections.heading: Where findings come from
sections.text:
Every finding carries an origin, because the origin decides how it can be checked.
Origin | How it is made | Who or what does the work
Stated | Pulled out of a written report or deck: the claims the authors themselves make | A model reads the document and extracts the claims. It is asked to quote, not to invent.
Generated | Computed from a table in the cross tab workspace, for example a column that differs from the rest of its banner variable | Code. The figures and the significance test come from the data, not from a model.
Coded | Produced by the qualitative analysis, for example a code that appears on two or more participant turns | The coding pipeline described in the qualitative guide.
Findings are also tagged quantitative or qualitative, which is what the filter at the top of the Findings tab uses. A stated finding can be either, since a report may quote a statistic or a theme.
Findings from tables
Table findings are the cleanest because nothing is paraphrased. The wording is built from the table itself: the figure, its base, and the test used. Tables are only turned into findings once you commit them. Findings from a starter set are also filtered with a false discovery rate correction, because so many cells are tested at once. Cells on a base under 30 respondents are never turned into findings, because the figure would not be dependable enough to state. The cross tab guide explains the test and the base rules in detail.
Findings from documents
Stated findings depend on a model reading prose, so they carry more risk. Models can drop a qualifier, merge two sentences, or restate a number slightly differently (Ji et al., 2023). That is why every stated finding is linked to its source passage and why verification, covered below, treats them more cautiously than generated ones.

sections.heading: Reviewing by exception
sections.text:
New findings arrive as accepted, not pending. A run can easily produce well over a hundred of them, and nobody reads each one before the next stage can run. So the workflow is the reverse of an approval queue: you scan, and you reject the ones that are wrong, duplicated or irrelevant. Rejected findings are kept, not deleted, and drop out of everything built downstream.
- Accepted: in play, and eligible to feed verification and insights.
- Rejected: set aside. Still visible, and recoverable if you change your mind.
- Adjusted: you can change a finding's kind, theme or note. The source link stays.
"Regenerate rejected" replaces only the findings you rejected and leaves everything accepted, and whatever has been built on it, untouched. If findings are about to be removed in a way that cannot be avoided (reprocessing a document, deleting a table), a snapshot is archived first so the earlier version can still be looked up.

sections.heading: Duplicates and look-alikes
sections.text:
The same number often appears in a report and again in the deck built from it. The app compares findings by how much of their wording overlaps and flags the pairs that look like the same claim. It is a cheap, no-model comparison, and it is intentionally modest: it says "these look alike, take a look". It does not decide whether two statements come from independent research, because that is a judgement about provenance that wording alone cannot settle.
Flagged duplicates matter for the next step. A claim repeated across two documents is not the same as a claim confirmed by two studies, and the app tries not to confuse them.

sections.heading: Verification: the four verdicts
sections.text:
Verification asks a narrow question of each finding: is the evidence behind it adequate for the claim as worded? It does not ask whether the finding is interesting. The answer is one of four verdicts.
Verdict | Meaning | Feeds insights?
Robust | The evidence supports the claim as stated, with no material concerns | Yes
Use with caution | Probably sound, but with a stated caveat such as a small base or a single source | Yes, and the caveat travels with it
Not supported | The evidence does not support the claim, or conflicts with it | No
Insufficient information | There is not enough in the material to judge either way | No
The route to a verdict depends on the origin. Generated findings are judged by code, because the numbers are right there: the check looks at the base sizes behind the figure and applies informal bands around n=30 and n=50. Stated and coded findings are judged by a model, working through them in batches of 20 with a ceiling of 100 per pass, and asked to look at plausibility and at contradictions with the other material. The model proposes the verdict and a reason, and the reason is stored so you can read why.
Why it works this way
Where a rule can be written down, it is done in code, not by a model. Base sizes, counts of sources and the corroboration status are all computed. The model is used only for the part that needs reading and judgement, and its output is checked for shape before anything is stored.

sections.heading: Caveat tags
sections.text:
A verdict is a summary. The caveat tags say what pulled it down, and they are worth reading before you rely on a finding.
Tag | What it is telling you
Base size small / borderline / unknown | The group behind the figure is small, near the threshold, or the base was not stated
Standard deviation unknown | A mean or difference was reported without a spread, so its reliability cannot be judged
Uncorrected multiple comparisons | Many cells were tested at once and none was adjusted (no correction chosen, or a check that does not correct, such as a banner plan), so a few will look significant by chance
False discovery controlled (row) | The finding survived a Benjamini-Hochberg correction across the columns of its banner variable, the cross tab default
Bonferroni corrected (row) | The finding survived the stricter Bonferroni correction, when that was chosen
False discovery rate controlled within table | The finding survived a Benjamini-Hochberg correction across every cell tested in its table
Survey design modelled | The test used the PSU and strata named for the data file (Taylor series variance)
Sampling assumed random | No survey design was modelled, so the test treats the sample as random, which may not hold for the survey design
Insufficient n for a test | There were too few cases for a significance test to mean anything
The multiple comparisons tag deserves particular attention in cross tab work. Test enough cells and a few will cross the 95% line by luck alone. An adjustment such as the false discovery rate procedure (Benjamini & Hochberg, 1995) is a recognised remedy. Every cross table applies one by default, whether it came from StarterTabs or was built by hand: the false discovery rate across the columns of each banner variable, row by row. Bonferroni, or no correction, can be chosen instead, and the finding's tag says which ran. Findings from the starter set are also controlled across every cell of their table. A table built with no correction carries the uncorrected tag. Even with a correction, treat a lone significant cell inside a very large table with some suspicion, and prefer patterns that show up across several related cells.

sections.heading: Corroboration and contradiction
sections.text:
Beyond each finding on its own, the app records how it relates to the rest of the evidence. Corroboration is decided in code from the links between findings: whether the same claim appears in more than one source, and whether one finding is grounded by another. The result is one of cross-source corroborated, single source, or contradicted.
Stated insights, meaning the interpretations a report offers, are tested separately against the evidence the app holds. If the app's own evidence conflicts with a claim in a report, that claim is pulled down to not supported, whatever it scored before, and the earlier reasoning is kept alongside so nothing is lost.
Reading a verdict
A report says 62% of informal traders save weekly. The table behind it shows the figure on 41 respondents. The verdict is likely to be "use with caution", tagged base size borderline. It still feeds insight generation, but the caution is attached and visible when someone reads the insight later.

sections.heading: Limitations
sections.text:
Limitation: A verdict is a judgement, not a proof
"Robust" means the evidence in the material supports the claim as worded. It does not mean the claim is true of the world. A well-supported claim from a poorly designed study is still well supported on the page and weak in practice. Statistical significance in particular is a narrow statement and is easily over-read (Wasserstein & Lazar, 2016).
Limitation: Model-judged verdicts can vary
Verdicts on stated and coded findings come from a model. Run twice, a borderline case may land in a neighbouring tier. The stored reason lets you disagree sensibly, and you can always override by rejecting a finding.
Limitation: Extraction can lose nuance
Atomising a claim means a hedge or condition in the original sentence can be dropped. Check the source link on anything that matters before you quote it.
Limitation: Corroboration is not independence
Two documents repeating the same underlying survey count as one source of evidence, not two, but the app can only detect that when the findings look alike or are linked. Provenance you know about and the app does not is worth adding in a note.
Limitation: Table findings inherit table limits
They use a complement comparison (a column against everyone else in the same banner variable), corrected only within the row (or the table) under the setting chosen, and a survey design only when one was named; their caveats say which. The correction does not cover the many tables of a project. Treat them as leads to examine, not as confirmed differences.
What this does
- Splits sources into atomic claims, each linked to where it came from.
- Computes table findings from the data, with the base and test stated.
- Rates each finding on evidence adequacy and attaches caveat tags.
- Flags look-alike findings and records corroboration and contradiction.
- Keeps rejected and archived findings so history is recoverable.
What this does not do
- Prove that a claim is true in the real world.
- Decide whether two similar findings come from independent research.
- Correct for multiple comparisons across the many tables of a project (each table is corrected on its own).
- Judge whether a finding is interesting or useful. That is the next stage.

sections.heading: A sensible way to work with it
sections.text:
- Skim the Findings tab with the quantitative and qualitative filters, and reject what is wrong or irrelevant.
- Open the source link on anything surprising, since surprises are where extraction errors hide.
- Run verification and read the caveat tags, not only the verdict.
- Look at findings marked contradicted or single source before you rely on them.
- Only then move to insights. Findings that are not supported will not carry through, by design.

sections.text:
