pages.title: How insights are made and tested
pages.blurb: From verified findings to synthesised insights, the six-point gate, confidence, and where they stop

sections.heading: Introduction
sections.text:
How insights are made and tested
How verified findings become insights, what the synthesis step and its gate do, how confidence and quality are worked out, and where the method stops. It describes current behaviour and will change as the app does.
Method guides · about 11 minute read · updated 2026-10-08

sections.heading: What an insight is
sections.text:
A finding says what the evidence shows. An insight says what it means and why it matters. The test the app applies is demanding: an insight should be supported by the evidence, not obvious, name a tension, and point to something someone could do. A statement that merely restates a number does not qualify, however accurate it is.
Each insight in the app has four parts. A headline you could say in a sentence. An observation that states what the evidence shows. A tension, the thing that pulls two ways or does not add up, which is what makes it more than a fact. And an implication, what follows for the decision at hand.
Finding versus insight
Finding: "Most small traders say they trust mobile money, yet most keep their working cash in a tin." That is two facts side by side.
Insight: trust is not the barrier, so campaigns that build trust will probably not move behaviour. What may matter instead is how easily money moves back to cash when a supplier needs paying on the spot. The tension is between stated trust and revealed behaviour, and the implication is to test cash-out convenience before spending on reassurance.

sections.heading: What goes in
sections.text:
Only findings that passed verification as robust or use with caution feed insight generation. Not supported and insufficient information findings are left out, as are rejected ones. That filter matters: whatever weakness a finding has is carried forward into anything built on it, so the app stops it at the door.
The insights stage also reads the framing you gave the run: the research objective, the business problem and, where one exists, the decision to be made. The more specific that framing is, the more targeted the insights will be.

sections.heading: Step one: a pre-insight for each finding
sections.text:
For each eligible finding, a model drafts one pre-insight with the four parts above. This is done in batches of 15, up to 60 findings per pass. At this point the app has a lot of candidates and no judgement about which deserve to be kept: a pre-insight is a working note, not a conclusion. Many will be near the surface, because a single finding rarely supports much interpretation on its own.
Why it works this way
Going one finding to one insight produces a data dump. Ninety findings in and seventy-five "insights" out means nothing was generalised or selected. The second step exists to force that selection.

sections.heading: Generate or validate
sections.text:
A run starts in one of two modes, and the mode changes the order of work.
Mode | Starting point | What happens
Generate | You have data and no fixed question yet | Insights are drawn from the evidence first. A decision is proposed afterwards, and you confirm or change it.
Validate | You already know the decision, usually from a brief | The decision is confirmed first and recorded as the decision context. Insights are written and filtered against it.
Generate mode is better for exploring a new dataset. Validate mode is better when a client has a clear question, because relevance can be judged against something specific. The cost of generate mode is that interesting but unrelated insights can crowd the list.

sections.heading: Step two: synthesis
sections.text:
Synthesis turns many pre-insights into fewer, stronger insights. It has three stages.
- Cluster. One model call sees every eligible pre-insight together (up to 60) and groups them the way you would group sticky notes on a wall: by shared underlying pattern, not by topic label. It has to see them all at once, because patterns across themes are only visible when everything is in view. Decision relevance is deliberately not applied here, since an early version that did so tended to exclude almost everything before grouping even began.
- Reframe and test. Each cluster with at least two members is reinterpreted around the tension that connects its members, then checked against the six-point gate below, plus a materiality test: would the decision change if this insight went away? A cluster of one is not promoted, because nothing has been compared against anything.
- Record. This stage is plain code. It counts how many pre-insights back each insight and how many distinct themes they come from, links the insight to every pre-insight behind it, and works out a confidence tier from the counts.
A cluster that fails the gate is simply not promoted. Its pre-insights stay visible and nothing is deleted, so you can see what was considered and left behind. Synthesis is also incremental: a later pass only clusters pre-insights that have not been used yet. It will not quietly rewrite insights you have already reviewed or built recommendations on.

sections.heading: The six-point gate
sections.text:
Test | The question it asks
Evidence-grounded | Does the claim follow from the findings behind it, and nothing beyond them?
Non-obvious | Would a reasonable reader already have guessed it? A truism fails.
Names a tension | Does it explain something that pulls two ways, rather than restate a fact?
Feels true | Would someone who knows this audience recognise it?
Actionable | Does a concrete next step follow? If not, it must be explicitly kept as no action.
Communicable | Can it be said in one or two sentences?
The "actionable" test has a deliberate exit. An insight that is real and well evidenced but has no sensible action is kept and marked retained, no action, so it is not forced into a made-up recommendation. Insights with a clear next step are marked has action.

sections.heading: Confidence and thin evidence
sections.text:
Confidence is worked out by counting, not by asking the model how sure it is. Two numbers drive it: how many pre-insights support the insight (triangulation), and how many different themes they come from.
Tier | Rule
Strong | Supported by at least three pre-insights, drawn from at least two themes
Moderate | Either at least two themes, or at least three pre-insights, but not both
Exploratory | Neither: a small cluster from a single theme
An insight resting on the bare minimum of two supporting pre-insights carries a Thin evidence badge. Losing one finding could undo it. A fuller reproducibility check is available too: the app drops a quarter of the evidence at random, re-runs the grouping five times, and looks at whether the same insight reappears with at least half of its surviving members together. An insight that keeps reappearing is less likely to be an accident of one particular grouping. If every resample removes too much of its evidence, the result is reported as inconclusive, which is not a failure.

sections.heading: Quality scores
sections.text:
Separately from the verdict on the underlying finding, each pre-insight is scored on how good an insight it actually is. There are five dimensions, each scored 1, 3 or 5: why (does it explain), actionability, novelty, synthesis (does it bring things together) and evidentiary proportionality (does the explanation stay within what the finding shows). The total runs from 5 to 25 and maps to a tier.
Total | Tier | Reading
15 or more | Qualified | A real insight
12 to 14 | Partial | Promising, needs sharpening
Under 12 | Finding | Still essentially a restated observation
Scoring never deletes or hides anything. A low score pushes an insight down the list and is a prompt to sharpen or drop it, but the decision stays with you. Recommendations built from insights have their own score on actionability, feasibility and evidence, with impact shown alongside but kept out of the total.

sections.heading: Accepting and rejecting
sections.text: Insights are reviewed, not just produced. You can accept an insight, reject it, or leave it pending, and the status decides what flows on to recommendations and reports. Rejected insights stay visible rather than disappearing, and every insight keeps its links to the findings underneath it.

sections.heading: Limitations
sections.text:
Limitation: The interpretation is a model's proposal
Naming a tension is an act of interpretation, and a model will find one if asked, even where the evidence is thin. Language models can produce fluent, confident text that is not well grounded in their inputs (Bender et al., 2021; Ji et al., 2023). The gate and the counts reduce that risk. They do not remove it, which is why every insight links back to its findings and why reading those findings is part of the job.
Limitation: Triangulation counts are not independence
Three supporting pre-insights may all come from one report or one survey. The count shows how many pieces of evidence agree, not whether they were gathered independently. The theme count helps, but it is a rough proxy.
Limitation: Clustering is not perfectly repeatable
Run again, the grouping can shift, particularly for borderline patterns. That is the reason for the reproducibility check, and also a reason to be wary of an insight that appears in one run and never again.
Limitation: Association is not cause
Most evidence here is correlational. An insight that implies a cause ("trust is not the barrier") is a hypothesis to test. Causal claims need more than co-occurrence; classic criteria such as consistency, plausibility and temporality are a useful checklist (Hill, 1965), and a pilot or experiment is better still.
Limitation: Readers have biases too
An insight that fits what stakeholders already believe will be accepted too easily, and one that cuts against them will be questioned harder than the evidence deserves (Nickerson, 1998). Reviewers should apply the same scrutiny both ways, including to insights that please them.
Limitation: Framing shapes the output
In validate mode, relevance is judged against the decision you gave. A poorly framed decision produces well-evidenced answers to the wrong question.
What this does
- Uses only verified findings, and carries their caveats forward.
- Groups related evidence and promotes only patterns that pass the six-point gate.
- Counts support in code and shows confidence, thin evidence and stability.
- Scores insight quality as a separate axis from evidence quality.
- Keeps rejected insights and unpromoted pre-insights visible.
What this does not do
- Establish cause, or tell you what the client should do. It proposes, you decide.
- Guarantee that supporting evidence is independent.
- Replace reading the underlying findings and sources.
- Delete anything on a low score.

sections.heading: A sensible way to work with it
sections.text:
- Fix the framing first. Write the decision or objective as precisely as you can.
- Review and verify findings before generating insights. Fixing a bad finding later costs more.
- Read each insight alongside its supporting findings. Ask whether the tension is really in the evidence.
- Treat thin evidence and exploratory tiers as questions worth testing, not conclusions.
- Run the reproducibility check on the insights you intend to lead with.
- Accept, reject or edit, then move on to recommendations with only the insights you would defend.

pages.title: How decisions are framed and linked to evidence
pages.blurb: Two-pass candidate proposals, how decisions link to objectives and insights, the review workflow, and where they stop

sections.heading: Introduction
sections.text:
How decisions are framed and linked to evidence
What the decision brief is, how candidate decisions are proposed from your evidence, how they connect to objectives, insights and recommendations, and where the connection is looser than it may look. It describes current behaviour and will change as the app does.
Method guides · about 11 minute read · updated 2026-10-08

sections.heading: What a decision brief is
sections.text:
The decision brief is the screen where a project states the choices its research is meant to inform. A decision here is a fork a stakeholder faces, with a real option on each side. "Whether to launch the loyalty tier in Q2 or hold until after the rebrand" is a decision. "Understand member attitudes to the loyalty programme" is a research question, and the framer is explicitly told not to produce those.
The wording matters more than it may seem. How a choice is framed can change what people prefer, even when the underlying options are the same (Tversky & Kahneman, 1981). Writing each decision as a named choice, not a yes/no question, is an attempt to keep the framing neutral between the options.
Why it works this way
Decisions give the later stages something to be judged against. Without one, a recommendation can only be general advice. With one, the app can ask whether an insight pushes toward one option, complicates the choice, or leaves it alone.

sections.heading: How candidates are proposed
sections.text:
Candidates are proposed by a model in two separate passes. They are kept apart on purpose. A decision written straight from finding-level facts tends to come out shaped like a research question, so the first pass states what the evidence shows and the second pass works from that statement.
- Synthesis. The model writes two to four sentences on what the evidence collectively points to, hedged, and connected to your business problem or research objective when you gave one. This is saved on the run and shown on the left of the screen as "What the evidence shows", so you can judge whether a candidate follows from it.
- Candidates. From that synthesis, the model proposes three to five decisions. Each comes with a short rationale naming the themes that bear on it and why a stakeholder would plausibly face the choice. It is told not to invent a decision the evidence has nothing to say about, and not to offer two candidates that are the same choice reworded.
The framer runs automatically once documents have been processed and findings exist. You can also trigger it yourself with the button on the screen, labelled "Get suggestions" the first time and "Regenerate suggestions" afterwards. A failure in the automatic run is logged and does not interrupt whatever you were doing. A failure from the button is shown on the screen.

sections.heading: What the framer reads
sections.text:
What it reads depends on how the project was started.
Project mode | Evidence the framer reads | If there is none
Generate (mining raw data) | Insights, each with its observation, tension and implication | It stops with an error. It does not fall back to raw findings, because the ordering of findings, then insights, then a decision is deliberate.
Validate (testing a report's claims) | Findings directly, since no insights exist yet at this point | It stops with an error asking for at least one document's worth of findings.
In both modes it is also given your business problem, your research objective and the intended audience, where you supplied them. It is told to treat the problem and objective as the strongest signal of what matters. If you gave neither, it works from the evidence alone and favours the more commercially concrete reading. At most 120 findings or insights are passed in, ordered by theme.
Your own upfront text is not treated as a decision. A business problem or an objective says why the research exists. It is rarely a choice between options. If you do have a decision in mind, add it yourself on the review screen.

sections.heading: How decisions link to objectives and insights
sections.text:
There are three kinds of link, and they differ in strength. It helps to know which is which.
Link | How it is made | How strong it is
Decision to evidence | The framer reads the evidence, writes a synthesis, and names themes in each rationale | Thematic. The rationale mentions themes, but no candidate is tied to specific finding or insight records.
Decision to objective | The framer reads the objective text on the run, and the validation step later lists objectives and decisions side by side | Textual. The framer reads the objective as a piece of text, not the accepted objective candidates as records.
Decision to insight | In validate mode, each insight is written in light of the accepted decisions and stores them as its decision context. After analysis, each decision is checked against the accepted synthesized insights | Judged by a model, and the result is stored with the insights it cites.
The disposition of each decision
Once synthesized insights have been accepted, the validation step takes every research objective and every accepted decision as a separate item and gives each one a status: resolved, partial, or gap. It also writes a short conclusion and records which insights it relied on. A decision that no accepted insight bears on is marked as a gap, which is a useful result in its own right. Decisions that came from the framer are flagged as inferred, so reports can show that their coverage is somewhat circular: the insights helped suggest the decision that they are then checked against.
Reading a gap
Suppose one accepted decision concerns pricing and none of your accepted insights touch price. The decision shows as a gap. Either the research did not cover pricing, or the framer proposed a decision the evidence could only loosely inform. The conclusion text and the rationale together usually show which.

sections.heading: The review workflow
sections.text:
Review works by exception, in the same spirit as findings. Every suggested decision lands already accepted, so the project can carry on without waiting for a click. You then edit, remove or add. More than one decision can be accepted at once, and a project can be organised around several.
Action | What it does
Edit, then Save and accept | Changes the wording and marks the candidate as edited. Edited candidates are protected from being replaced when suggestions are regenerated.
Reject (on a candidate that is not accepted) | Moves it to a collapsed Rejected list, where it is kept and can be restored. Rejecting one never affects the others.
Restore | Puts a rejected candidate back as accepted.
Accept all / Delete all | Applies to every candidate that is still pending. Deleting is permanent.
Delete | Removes a candidate for good. If it was accepted, the project decision statement is rebuilt from whatever remains accepted.
Add your own decision | Writes a candidate labelled Your text, accepted straight away.
Behind the screen, the accepted candidates are joined into one decision statement for the project. With a single accepted decision it is that text. With several, it becomes a numbered list. That statement is what the downstream stages read.

sections.heading: Regenerating suggestions
sections.text:
Regenerating replaces the framer's earlier suggestions with a fresh batch. It removes suggested candidates that you have not edited, whether pending or accepted, and leaves alone anything you rejected, anything you edited, and anything you wrote yourself. The removal and the new insert happen together, so a failed attempt leaves the earlier list as it was. If the model returns nothing usable, you see an error and nothing changes.
The new batch is also told which decisions are already accepted and asked not to restate them. Since that list can include suggestions about to be replaced, a regenerated set may drift away from the first set even when the evidence has not changed. If a particular candidate matters, edit it or write it yourself so it is kept.

sections.heading: What changes when a decision is accepted
sections.text:
- Insights, validate mode. Insight generation waits for a decision. Once one is accepted, insights are generated against it, and each stores the decision text it was judged against.
- Insights, generate mode. Insights were already produced earlier without a decision, so accepting one mainly changes what comes after.
- Recommendations. In both modes, recommendations need a confirmed decision. Each action is written to serve the accepted decision or decisions.
- Objective and decision coverage. The dispositions described above are produced from the accepted decisions and the accepted synthesized insights.
Accepting, restoring, adding or editing a decision triggers a refresh of insights and recommendations. Rejecting or deleting one updates the decision statement but, as the code stands, does not trigger that refresh, so downstream items may still reflect the earlier set until the next analysis run.

sections.heading: Where it stops
sections.text:
Limitation: The link to evidence is thematic
A rationale names themes. It does not point to the particular findings or insights behind a candidate, so you cannot click through from a decision to its supporting records. Judging whether a candidate really follows from the evidence means reading the synthesis and the themes yourself.
Limitation: Model proposals can be plausible and wrong
Both passes are written by a model, which can overstate, merge or misread (Ji et al., 2023). The only checks on the output are that each candidate has non-empty text and a rationale. Nothing verifies that a candidate is genuinely a choice between options, or that the wording avoids favouring one side.
Limitation: The framer may read evidence you have set aside
From the queries it uses, the framer does not appear to filter findings or insights by review status or verdict. A finding you rejected, or one rated not supported, may still shape the synthesis. Treat the synthesis as a reading of everything extracted, not only of what you accepted.
Limitation: Coverage of large projects is partial
Only 120 items are read, ordered by theme, so on a large project later themes may not be seen at all. The synthesis cannot be assumed to represent the whole body of evidence.
Limitation: Auto-accepted does not mean endorsed
Suggestions arrive accepted so that work is not blocked, which means an unreviewed suggestion can steer recommendations. Skimming the list is worth doing early. It is easy to anchor on whichever framing arrives first and then read the evidence in its favour (Nickerson, 1998).
Limitation: Taking back an acceptance is awkward
On a candidate that is already accepted, the controls are Edit, Unaccept and Delete. From the code, Unaccept appears to call the same action as Restore, which sets a candidate to accepted, so it may not change anything. Deleting is the dependable way to remove an accepted candidate, and it is permanent.
Limitation: Circular coverage
In generate mode, decisions are suggested from the insights and then checked against the same insights. A resolved status on a suggested decision is weaker evidence than one on a decision you or a client stated independently.
What this does
- Proposes three to five decisions from a stated synthesis of the evidence, each with a rationale.
- Shows the synthesis so the reasoning can be checked.
- Lets you accept, edit, reject, restore, delete or add decisions, with several active at once.
- Passes the accepted decisions to insight generation, recommendations and coverage checks.
- Keeps your edited, rejected and self-written candidates through a regenerate.
What this does not do
- Know which decision your client actually faces. Only you can supply that.
- Link a candidate to specific findings or insight records.
- Check that a candidate is a real choice, or that its wording is neutral.
- Exclude rejected or unsupported evidence from the synthesis.
- Prove that the evidence is enough to settle a decision. A resolved status is a model judgement.

sections.heading: A sensible way to work with it
sections.text:
- Fill in the business problem and research objective before processing, since they carry the most weight.
- Read "What the evidence shows" first, and ask whether you would have said the same.
- Go through each candidate and check that it is a choice with two real sides. Edit the wording where it is not.
- Delete or reject candidates that belong to no real stakeholder, and add the ones the framer missed.
- After the insights are accepted, read the resolved, partial and gap statuses, and look hardest at the gaps.

pages.blurb: Asking from any page, what it reads, how-the-app questions from the guides, answering data questions with draft tables you can open, sample sizes and margins of error from a tested calculator, method advice, report edits, and where it stops

sections.heading: Introduction
sections.text:
How the Research assistant works
What the assistant reads, how it answers questions about your data with tables you can open, how it works out sample sizes and margins of error, and where its answers should be checked. It describes current behaviour and will change as the app does.
Method guides · about 9 minute read · updated 2026-10-22

sections.heading: What the assistant is for
sections.text:
The Research assistant is a chat for one project, under Tools, and from the Ask the assistant button on every page. It answers questions about the project's accepted evidence and report, answers questions about the project's data by building cross tables, explains how the app works from this Knowledge base and the Manual, gives general research advice, and rewrites a part of the Insights Report when you ask.
Why it works this way
A model is good at planning and explaining and unreliable at arithmetic. So the assistant plans the table and the app builds it; it chooses the inputs for a sample size and the app works it out. Any figure it quotes about your data or your sample should trace back to a table or a calculation you can see.

sections.heading: Asking from any page
sections.text:
The Ask the assistant button sits in the bottom-right corner of every page. It opens the assistant in a panel on the right, so the page you are working on stays in view. Esc or the close button puts it away.
- Inside a project it is the same conversation as the Research assistant section, saved with the project, and it is told which section you asked from, so "what does this mean?" on Findings is read as a question about Findings. The button is hidden on the Research assistant section itself, where the conversation is already on the page.
- Outside a project (the dashboard, Programs, this Knowledge base, the Manual) it answers questions about how the app works and about research method. It has no project data there, and the chat is not saved: it lasts until the browser tab is closed or reloaded.
A question that cannot be answered (a lost connection, an error) stays in the panel of the project you asked it in, with the reason and a Send again button, also after you move to another page and back (not after a reload). When the connection drops, the answer may already have been saved: the panel reads the project's conversation again and shows the saved answer if it is there. Sending a question again never stores it twice; an answer already saved is shown instead of being asked again. An answer that was cut off for length, or came back empty, is not shown: the assistant says so and asks you to ask again.

sections.heading: What it reads
sections.text: Each message is answered from the project's business problem, objective, decision statement and audience, the generated report narrative if there is one, accepted insights and recommendations, the objective coverage statuses, and accepted findings rated robust or use with caution. Larger projects are cut to the first 80 findings, 60 insights and 40 recommendations. The last 20 messages of the conversation go with it, so a follow-up such as "and by region?" is read in context.

sections.heading: Questions about how the app works
sections.text: For a question about a screen, a method or a limit, the assistant searches the Knowledge base and the Manual and reads the sections that fit, then answers from them. The reply ends with a line naming the guides it read, with links, so you can read the source yourself. When the guides do not cover something, it is told to say so rather than describe behaviour it has not read.

sections.heading: Questions about the data
sections.text:
When a question needs figures, the assistant lists the project's data files, searches their variables, and asks for a table. The request goes through the same checks as SemanticTabs: every variable must exist in the file, and filters must use real categories. The table is then built by the same engine as every other cross table, with the file's weight unless you ask for unweighted figures, and with its saved survey design for the significance tests.
Each table is saved as a draft under Cross tabs, All tables, with a Research assistant badge. The reply ends with a line naming the tables built for it, so you can open the table, check the base and the marks, and then commit it into findings or delete it. At most four tables are built for one message.
Example
"Is satisfaction different by gender?" builds Overall satisfaction by Gender. The reply quotes the shares from that table, says whether it was weighted, and calls a difference significant only when the table marks it.
If a step fails (the variables cannot be read, the design set-up cannot be read, a variable does not exist), the assistant is told so and no table is built. It is not given a default design or weight in place of the one that could not be read.

sections.heading: Sample sizes and margins of error
sections.text:
Questions such as "what sample do I need for a 5% margin of error?" or "what is the margin of error on 400 interviews?" are worked out by a calculator in the app, and the reply shows its working and assumptions. The method is the standard one for a proportion (Cochran, 1977), with one model used in both directions, so the sample size for a margin gives that margin back:
- The margin for n interviews: e = z × √(deff × p × (1 − p) ÷ n), with p = 50% unless you give an expected share.
- The design effect (deff) for clustered or weighted samples (Kish, 1965) sits inside the variance; it is 1 for a simple random sample.
- With a known population N, the margin is multiplied by √((N − n) ÷ (N − 1)).
- The sample for a margin is that formula solved for n: n0 = z² × deff × p × (1 − p) ÷ e², then n0 ÷ (1 + (n0 − 1) ÷ N) when N is known, rounded up. That is the smallest sample whose margin is at most e, and it is never more than the population.
- Divided by a response rate, it gives the number of people to approach; when that is more people than the population holds, the calculator says so instead of giving a number.
Reference values the calculator is tested against (95% confidence, p = 50%)
Question | Answer
Interviews for a 5% margin | 385
Interviews for a 3% margin | 1,068
Interviews for a 5% margin, population 1,000 | 278
Interviews for a 5% margin, design effect 1.5 | 577
Interviews for a 5% margin, design effect 2, population 1,000 | 435
Margin on 1,000 interviews | ±3.1 points
Margin on 400 interviews | ±4.9 points
A value the calculator cannot use, such as a confidence level other than 90, 95 or 99 percent, or a figure sent as words, is refused with the reason rather than replaced by a default.
Confidence can be 90, 95 or 99 percent. The margin applies to the whole sample: a subgroup you plan to report on its own, such as one province, needs its own sample size, and the assistant is told to say so.

sections.heading: General research advice
sections.text: The assistant also answers method questions as a methodologist would: questionnaire wording, sampling, weighting, significance testing, qualitative approaches. It is told to say when advice is general practice rather than drawn from this project, and to name the assumptions it rests on.

sections.heading: Changes to the report
sections.text: Asked to shorten, tighten or rewrite a part of the Insights Report (the executive summary, a pillar's headline, the caveats), the assistant writes new text for exactly that part. Fields you did not mention are left alone.

sections.heading: Where it stops
sections.text:
Limitation: The wording is still a model's
The figures come from tables, but the sentence around them is written by a model, which can misread or overstate (Ji et al., 2023). Open the table named at the end of the reply before quoting a figure.
Limitation: A margin of error assumes a probability sample
For a quota or opt-in panel sample there is no sampling margin in the strict sense. The calculator's figure then describes the precision a random sample of that size would have, not the error of your survey. It covers a proportion, not a mean.
Limitation: Design effects are your estimate
The calculator uses the design effect you give, or 1. It does not estimate one from your data, so a clustered or heavily weighted sample will look more precise than it is unless you supply a realistic figure.
Limitation: Long projects are read in part
Only the capped numbers of findings, insights and recommendations are read, so a question about a late theme on a large project may get "not covered".
Limitation: Guide search matches words
The guides are searched by the words in the question, not their meaning, so a question worded very differently from the guide may not find it. Asking again with the term the app uses usually does.
Limitation: Outside a project nothing is kept
The chat outside a project is not saved. Its use is counted for your organisation and shown on the dashboard (the last 30 days, with the part read from the cache and an estimated cost), not on a project's API usage page, which counts only that project's calls.
Limitation: Drafts accumulate
Each data question can add up to four draft tables. They stay until you commit or delete them. A table saved whose figures could not be read back is still listed under the reply, marked as such, and counts towards the four.
What this does
- Builds the tables it quotes, through the same checks and engine as SemanticTabs, and saves them as drafts.
- Uses the file's weight and saved survey design, and stops when either cannot be read.
- Works out sample sizes and margins of error with a tested calculator and shows the working.
- Rewrites only the report fields you name.
- Answers how-the-app questions from the Knowledge base and Manual, and links the guides it read.
What this does not do
- Compute a figure itself, or guarantee its sentence matches the table it built.
- Estimate a design effect from your data.
- Give a margin of error that applies to a non-probability sample.
- Commit its tables into findings for you.

sections.heading: A sensible way to work with it
sections.text:
- Ask one question at a time, naming the variables and groups when you know them.
- Open each table listed at the end of the reply and check the base and whether it was weighted.
- For sample sizes, give the population, expected response rate and a design effect when you have them.
- Commit the tables worth keeping, and delete the rest from All tables.

pages.title: Start here
pages.blurb: What Insights Elevator is, and isn't

sections.heading: Introduction
sections.text:
Start here
A short, honest explanation of what Insights Elevator does, in plain terms, before any of the detail pages. If you only read one page in this manual, read this one.
Insights Elevator takes a research report or a dataset and turns it into a set of checked, traceable findings, insights, and recommendations. It does the reading, the cross-checking, and the organising. It does not do your thinking for you, and it is built to say so clearly whenever it is uncertain, rather than present every output with the same confidence.

sections.heading: The two ways to start
sections.text:
Generate from data starts from raw tables or a dataset with no existing findings. The app reads through it directly and looks for patterns worth reporting.
Validate existing insights starts from a report that already makes claims, a deck, a write-up, a set of slides. The app checks each claim against the evidence actually supplied, rather than taking the report's own conclusions at face value.

sections.heading: The one idea that runs through everything else
sections.text:
Every finding, insight, and recommendation in this app carries a status: pending, accepted, or rejected, and a trail back to the exact document or table it came from. Nothing is presented as settled just because the system produced it. A finding stays pending until a person has looked at it, and a rejected finding is kept, not deleted, so the record of what was considered and set aside is never lost.
Why it works this way
An AI system that reads documents and draws conclusions from them can make mistakes, the same way a junior analyst can. The honest response to that is not to pretend it never happens, it is to build a process that catches it: statistical checks run automatically, every claim keeps its source, and a person reviews before anything is treated as final. That review step is the actual safeguard. The rest of this manual explains how each part of it works.
What this does
- Extracts claims from your material and checks them against the evidence actually supplied
- Runs statistical checks (margin of error, base-size flags, significance tests) automatically
- Shows its working: every output traces back to a specific document, table, or finding
- Groups related findings into a smaller number of genuinely useful, cross-cutting insights
What this does not do
- Guarantee a finding is correct just because it passed a check: checks catch specific, known failure modes, not every possible error
- Replace your own judgment about whether a recommendation is the right call for your organisation
- Treat every table the same way: raw, respondent-level data is deliberately handled more carefully than an already-summarised table (see Raw data and banner plans)

sections.heading: How to use this manual
sections.text:
The pages in the sidebar run in roughly the order your material moves through the app: upload, extraction, verification, raw data if you have it, insights, recommendations, and the audit trail. The last two pages, what this doesn't do and the glossary, are reference material you can jump to at any point.
For more room on any screen, hide the main menu on the far left with the arrow beside the Insights Elevator name; the arrow on the narrow strip that remains shows it again. Your browser remembers the choice.

pages.title: Uploading your material
pages.blurb: Reports, tables, and transcripts

sections.heading: Introduction
sections.text:
Uploading your material
What you can upload, the one question that matters most, and what happens to your files.

sections.heading: Three kinds of document
sections.text:
Reports are narrative documents: a Word file, a PDF, a slide deck, anything written in prose that makes claims you want checked.
Tables are structured data: a spreadsheet, a CSV, or a Word/PDF document that contains one or more data tables worth analysing on their own terms. SPSS (.sav) and Stata (.dta) files are read the same way as a spreadsheet, including the variable and value labels they carry, so a question coded as Q7a with answers coded 1 and 2 shows up with its real label and category names rather than raw codes.
Transcripts are interview or focus-group material, read for claims the same way a report is, but kept in their own category since they carry a different kind of evidence (what someone said) than a report's own stated conclusions.

sections.heading: Raw or aggregated: the question that changes everything downstream
sections.text:
When you upload a table, you are asked whether it is aggregated (already summarised, for example a cross-tab with totals and percentages) or raw (one row per respondent, the kind of file a survey platform exports before anyone has summarised it).
This single choice decides how the table gets processed. An aggregated table is scanned automatically for patterns. A raw table is not scanned automatically at all; it waits for you to name which columns matter, through a banner plan. The Raw data and banner plans page explains exactly why, but the short version: scanning every possible pair of columns in a large raw file for anything interesting is a well-known way to generate false positives, so the app deliberately does not do that without your say in which comparisons are actually worth running.
Example
A 40-question customer survey with 2,000 respondents has 40 columns. Scanning every pair of columns means testing roughly 780 comparisons. At the standard 5% significance threshold, chance alone would produce around 39 "significant" results even if nothing real were happening in the data at all. That is the exact risk the raw/aggregated distinction exists to manage.
Why it works this way
Getting this one choice wrong in the safe direction (marking aggregated data as raw) costs you an extra step of naming your columns. Getting it wrong in the other direction (marking raw, respondent-level data as aggregated) risks a page full of statistically fragile, uncorrected findings presented as though they were solid. The app is built to make the safer mistake the default and the costlier one require a second, explicit choice.
What this does
- Reads CSV, Excel (.xlsx/.xls), SPSS (.sav) and Stata (.dta) files for tables; SAS is excluded pending verification
- Keeps every tenant's documents and data completely separate from every other tenant's
- Lets you re-upload or re-tag a document if you set the wrong kind or ingestion type the first time
What this does not do
- Guess whether your table is raw or aggregated for you: you have to say
- Read scanned, image-only PDFs: a table extraction pass needs actual selectable text
- Share evidence between different clients' runs, even inside the same organisation's account

pages.title: How findings are extracted
pages.blurb: Turning documents into checkable claims

sections.heading: Introduction
sections.text:
How findings are extracted
Turning a document into a list of checkable claims, and why that first pass is a reading task, not a fixed rule.

sections.heading: What a "finding" actually is
sections.text: A finding is one atomic, factual or statistical claim pulled out of your material: a statistic, a stated relationship, a described pattern. One document can produce many findings. Each finding keeps a link back to exactly where it came from, the specific document or table, so nothing in the system is ever a claim floating free of its source.

sections.heading: This is a reading task, not a parser
sections.text:
Extracting findings from narrative text or a transcript is done by an AI model reading the document, not by a fixed set of rules matching patterns in the text. That matters, because it means extraction is genuinely good at understanding context and phrasing, but it is not infallible the way a spreadsheet formula is. It can occasionally miss a claim, misread a number, or pull out something that is not actually a standalone finding.
Structured tables are different: a finding drawn from an aggregated table is computed, not read. The system runs an actual statistical test (a two-proportion comparison, a difference of means) against the numbers in the table itself, so a table-derived finding carries a real calculated result behind it, not a model's summary of one.

sections.heading: Every new finding starts as pending
sections.text:
A freshly extracted finding is never marked accepted by default. It sits as pending until the verification stage has assessed it and, ultimately, until a person has reviewed it. This is deliberate: the home page's reviewed count, and the "regenerate unreviewed" option, only mean something if pending genuinely means not yet looked at.
Why it works this way
Treating narrative extraction and table extraction differently is not an inconsistency, it is the point. A number computed directly from a table your data actually contains is a different kind of claim from a model's read of a sentence in a report, and the system is built to be honest about which kind each finding is, rather than presenting both with identical confidence.
What this does
- Pulls out specific, checkable claims rather than summarising a document in general terms
- Keeps a source link on every finding, back to the exact document or table it came from
- Runs an actual statistical test against table data, rather than describing it in prose
What this does not do
- Invent a finding not actually present in the source material: it extracts, it does not author new claims at this stage
- Guarantee every genuine claim in a long document was caught: a spot check against the source is worth doing on anything consequential
- Treat a narrative claim and a computed statistic as the same kind of evidence

pages.title: Verification and verdicts
pages.blurb: How each claim gets checked, and what the caveats mean

sections.heading: Introduction
sections.text:
Verification and verdicts
How each finding gets checked, what the four verdict tiers mean, and a plain-language reading of every caveat you'll see.

sections.heading: The four verdict tiers
sections.text:
Robust. The claim is well-supported by the evidence actually available in this run.
Use with caution. The claim has some support, but carries a real limitation worth knowing before you act on it, a small base size, an unverified sampling assumption, and so on.
Not supported. The evidence available does not back up the claim as stated.
Insufficient information. There simply isn't enough in the source material to judge the claim either way.

sections.heading: Caveats, in plain language
sections.text:
A caveat is a short, specific flag attached to a finding, telling you exactly what kind of limitation applies, rather than a vague warning. You'll see these as small badges on each pre-insight in the Insights tab. Here is what each one actually means:
sampling_assumed_random
The statistical test behind this finding assumes a simple random or quota sample: no survey design (PSU or strata) was named for its data file, or it came from a check that does not use one. Naming the design in Cross tabs makes its tables and NPS results design-based, see What this doesn't do yet.
base_size_small / base_size_borderline / base_size_unknown
The number of respondents behind this specific finding is small, on the edge of being usable, or simply wasn't stated. A finding built on 12 people deserves far less weight than one built on 1,200, even if both come out "statistically significant."
std_unknown
A report states a mean or average ("average satisfaction was 7.2") with no standard deviation, standard error, confidence interval, or range given alongside it. The figure is reported as stated, but how spread out the underlying scores actually were can't be assessed from this alone.
uncorrected_multiple_comparisons
This finding is one of several comparisons tested at once, and no statistical correction for that has been applied (no correction was chosen, or it came from a check that does not correct, such as the scan of an aggregated table or a banner plan). The more comparisons you run, the more likely one looks "significant" purely by chance. See the uploading page for a worked example of why this matters.
How to read a verdict in practice
"Customers in Region A are 15% more likely to churn than Region B", tagged use with caution with base_size_borderline and uncorrected_multiple_comparisons, means: the gap is real in this data, it came out of a batch of several comparisons so there's a real chance it's one of the occasional false positives that batch testing produces, and the group it's based on is on the small side. Worth a second look before it drives a decision on its own, not worth dismissing outright.
Why it works this way
A caveat is not an apology for the finding and it is not a reason to ignore it. It is the specific piece of context a careful human analyst would want before deciding how much weight to put on a number. Showing it by default, on every finding it applies to, is what lets you trust the findings that have no caveats attached at all.
What this does
- Recomputes margin of error and significance directly from the numbers in your source, rather than trusting a report's own stated figures
- Flags small or unstated base sizes, and a mean reported with no spread measure, automatically on every finding they apply to
- Shows every caveat as a visible badge on each pre-insight in the Insights tab, not just a value sitting unseen in the database
What this does not do
- Promise that a 'robust' verdict means the underlying research design itself was sound: it means the evidence actually supplied backs up the claim
- Apply a statistical correction for many comparisons in the scan of an aggregated table or a banner plan: that risk is disclosed via the caveat (cross tabs built in the app do correct, with a false discovery rate correction by default)
- Show these caveat badges on the raw pending-findings list before review, or on synthesized insights: those use their own separate checks

pages.title: Raw data and banner plans
pages.blurb: Why case-level data is handled differently

sections.heading: Introduction
sections.text:
Raw data and banner plans
Why a respondent-level dataset is not scanned automatically, and how to tell the app which comparisons you actually want.

sections.heading: The problem this solves
sections.text:
An already-aggregated table, a small cross-tab someone has already built, is safe to scan automatically for interesting patterns: there are only a handful of columns, and that kind of exploratory pass is standard, accepted practice in market research. A raw, respondent-level file is a different animal. It might have dozens or hundreds of columns, which means thousands of possible pairs to compare. Testing all of them automatically and reporting whatever comes out "significant" would produce a report full of findings that are, statistically, mostly noise dressed up as signal.
Example
Flip ten fair coins ten separate times. Purely by chance, one of those ten tries will probably land mostly heads. That run doesn't mean the coin is biased, it means that trying enough things eventually produces something that looks notable. Scanning every column pair in a large raw dataset is the statistical equivalent of running that coin-flip experiment hundreds of times and reporting every unusual-looking result as a finding.

sections.heading: What happens instead: a banner plan
sections.text:
When a table is flagged as raw, it is stored but not scanned. Instead, you tell the app which columns are the banner columns (the segmenting variables you actually want to compare across, like Gender or Age band) and which are the stub columns (the outcome measures you want to test against them, like satisfaction score or preferred channel). Naming a banner column compares every category inside it against every other by default, Male versus Female, say, which matches how a market-research tab plan is normally built: the discipline is in which columns you choose to name, not in restricting the pairs within one once you've named it.
Once you save a plan and click "Compute banner comparisons," the app runs an actual statistical test (a two-proportion comparison for categorical outcomes, a difference-of-means test for numeric ones) for every category pair in each banner column against each stub column, and only keeps the ones that come out statistically significant. Every result it keeps carries two caveats as standard: uncorrected_multiple_comparisons, because even a chosen, bounded set of comparisons still carries some of that same chance-finding risk, just at a scale you control, and sampling_assumed_random, for the reason explained below.

sections.heading: SPSS and Stata files
sections.text:
Initial release scope excludes columns-as-cases workbooks that require a separate Codebook to define weights or multiple-response sets, pending verification. Those definitions must not be assumed absent or replaced with an unweighted calculation. The app refuses analytical requests when that separate sheet declares those definitions. Re-export with one row per respondent and retain the Codebook, then upload again and verify the weight and multiple-response setup before calculating.
If your raw data comes from labelled statistical software, a .sav or .dta file (SAS is excluded pending verification), the app reads it directly, including the variable labels (so a column literally named Q7a shows up as "Preferred channel" if that's its label) and value labels (so a code like 1 shows up as "Male" rather than a bare number) wherever your file defines them.
Why it works this way
The banner plan does not model a survey design: its tests treat the sample as random, and each result says so with a caveat rather than quietly approximating a design. Cross tabs and the Net Promoter Score do model one, with Taylor series variance, when you name the PSU (cluster) and strata variables for the data file, so use those for a stratified or clustered sample. See What this doesn't do yet for what that means for your results today.
What this does
- Lets you name exactly which columns to compare, rather than scanning everything automatically
- Runs a real statistical test for every comparison it produces, not a guess or an estimate
- Reads SPSS and Stata files directly, labels and all
- Flags every banner-plan result as part of a multiple-comparisons batch, honestly, every time
What this does not do
- Scan a raw table automatically the way it does an aggregated one: that is a deliberate choice, not a missing feature
- Apply a statistical correction (like a Bonferroni adjustment) for the multiple comparisons a banner plan runs: the risk is disclosed, not adjusted away (cross tabs built in the app do correct, with a false discovery rate correction by default)
- Account for a survey design in a banner plan: it assumes a simple random or quota sample (cross tabs and NPS use the PSU and strata you name)

pages.title: Insights and synthesis
pages.blurb: From individual claims to the bigger picture

sections.heading: Introduction
sections.text:
Insights and synthesis
From one finding at a time to the smaller number of things actually worth telling someone.

sections.heading: Pre-insights: one per finding
sections.text: Every finding that is verified and accepted becomes one pre-insight. This is a direct, one-to-one translation, nothing is combined or reframed yet. Pre-insights are the complete, detailed layer, the full audit trail of everything the system found and checked.

sections.heading: Synthesized insights: the bigger picture
sections.text: A full report built from one insight per finding would usually be too long and too repetitive to actually use. Synthesis groups related pre-insights together and reframes each group into one higher-level, cross-cutting insight, the kind of observation a person would actually lead with in a meeting. Each synthesized insight has to clear a specific set of tests before it's kept: it has to be grounded in real evidence, say something non-obvious, name an actual tension rather than just restate a number, and be something you could plausibly act on or explicitly decide not to.

sections.heading: Why the final count is much smaller than the finding count
sections.text:
If a run produces 60 findings and surfaces 8 synthesized insights, that is not 52 findings being silently dropped. All 60 still exist as pre-insights, visible in the audit trail. The synthesis step is specifically designed to compress many related, overlapping findings into a small number of genuinely distinct, useful observations, the same way a good analyst would summarise a pile of data points into a handful of real takeaways rather than reading every number aloud.
Why it works this way
Quality scoring runs on both layers, pre-insights and synthesized insights, against a fixed rubric, so the system is checking its own synthesis work rather than assuming a grouped, reframed insight is automatically better just because it sounds more polished.
What this does
- Keeps every pre-insight, even ones not used in any synthesized insight, visible in the audit trail
- Only keeps a synthesized insight that clears an explicit, multi-point validity check
- Lets you re-run synthesis without silently reprocessing or rewriting insights you've already accepted
What this does not do
- Delete or hide a pre-insight just because it wasn't used in the final synthesized set
- Guarantee a synthesized insight is more important than one that stayed at the pre-insight level: synthesis groups for clarity, it doesn't rank by importance
- Produce identical synthesized insights on every rerun over the same material: see What this doesn't do yet for what's actually guaranteed about consistency

pages.title: Recommendations
pages.blurb: What gets proposed, and what's left to you

sections.heading: Introduction
sections.text:
Recommendations
What gets turned into a proposed action, and why the choice of what to actually do stays yours.

sections.heading: Two layers, matching the two insight layers
sections.text: Every pre-insight gets its own recommendation, part of the full audit trail. Every accepted synthesized insight also gets at least one recommendation of its own, the headline recommendations a client is actually meant to read. A synthesized insight can produce more than one recommendation if more than one genuinely distinct action is actually warranted; the system doesn't force a single action where two real ones exist.

sections.heading: What a recommendation actually contains
sections.text:
Each one includes the proposed action itself, a suggested owner role, a feasibility note, a timeline, a success metric, and the assumptions or risks behind it. The idea is a recommendation you could hand to someone and have them know what to do next, not a vague directional statement like "improve customer experience."
Why it works this way
A recommendation is a proposal built from the evidence, not a decision made on your behalf. It names a specific owner and a specific metric so it's easy to evaluate and easy to say no to, but the system has no visibility into your organisation's politics, capacity, or competing priorities, the things that actually decide whether a recommendation is the right call right now. That judgment is yours.
What this does
- Proposes a specific, owned, timed action for every surviving insight, with a stated success metric
- Allows more than one recommendation per insight when more than one distinct action is genuinely warranted
- Keeps the full recommendation set generated for every pre-insight, not only the headline ones
What this does not do
- Decide for you whether a recommendation is worth acting on: it proposes, you decide
- Know your organisation's internal constraints, budget, or politics: the feasibility note is a starting estimate, not a verified plan
- Guarantee the suggested owner role actually has authority over what's being asked: check that before assigning it

pages.title: The audit trail
pages.blurb: Nothing is deleted, everything stays traceable

sections.heading: Introduction
sections.text:
The audit trail
Why nothing in this app is ever silently deleted, and where to find it if it isn't.

sections.heading: Three tabs, three complete records
sections.text: Beneath the main report sits the working data section, split into three tabs: every pre-insight generated, every recommendation generated, and a history of anything removed or superseded. Each tab is computed in full regardless of which one you're currently looking at, so switching tabs never triggers new processing, it just changes what's shown.

sections.heading: What happens to a rejected finding
sections.text:
Rejecting a finding doesn't erase it. It moves into the history record, with the reason it was superseded or removed, so the fact that it was considered and why it didn't make the cut stays visible. If you re-run extraction or synthesis later, nothing that was already accepted gets silently regenerated or overwritten either: the system only processes material that is genuinely new since the last time it ran.
Why it works this way
A system whose core promise is trustworthy evidence has to hold its own internal record to the same standard. If a "regenerate" or "re-run" action could quietly erase or rewrite something you'd already reviewed and accepted, every review you'd ever done would be worth less than it looks. The audit trail exists specifically so that re-running a stage is always safe.
What this does
- Keeps a complete, append-only record of every finding, insight, and recommendation ever generated
- Shows exactly why something was removed or superseded, not just that it was
- Only reprocesses genuinely new material on a re-run, leaving already-accepted work untouched
What this does not do
- Permanently delete a finding when you reject it: it moves to history, it doesn't vanish
- Silently overwrite an accepted insight if you click re-run on an earlier stage
- Hide the fact that something was dropped: a drop is always a visible, explained event, never a quiet omission

pages.title: What this doesn't do yet
pages.blurb: The honest list of current boundaries

sections.heading: Introduction
sections.text:
What this doesn't do yet
A plain, consolidated list of real current boundaries. Trusting a system's output starts with knowing exactly where that trust should stop.

sections.heading: Initial import exclusions
sections.text: SAS files and columns-as-cases workbooks with a separate Codebook declaring weights or multiple-response sets are excluded pending verification. The latter combination is refused before analytical results are produced. Re-export with one row per respondent, retain the Codebook definitions, upload again and verify the weight and multiple-response setup. Removing those definitions to bypass the check is not a supported recovery.

sections.heading: No memory across engagements, yet
sections.text: Checking happens within a single run, against the material you've supplied for that run. There is no persistent store yet of everything a client has ever given you, which a new report could be cross-checked against. If a new report contradicts something from an earlier engagement, the system won't catch that on its own today.

sections.heading: No simulated respondents, bias auditor, or gap-finder
sections.text: The original design for this system includes agents that generate persona-grounded reactions to a draft narrative, audit for consumer-psychology and stakeholder cognitive biases, and identify what the original research didn't cover. None of those three are built yet. What exists today covers extraction, verification, insight generation, synthesis, and recommendations.

sections.heading: Survey design is modelled only where you name it
sections.text: Cross tabs and the Net Promoter Score take a survey design into account when you name a PSU (cluster) variable, and ideally a strata variable, for the data file: their variances use Taylor series linearisation and the result is tagged survey_design_modelled. Without a named design, and in the automatic scan of an aggregated table or a banner plan against raw data, every check (margin of error, significance tests, base-size flags) assumes a simple random or quota sample. Results are still computed and still useful, and they are tagged sampling_assumed_random to say so.

sections.heading: Correction for testing many things at once is not applied everywhere
sections.text: Cross tabs built in the app correct their column tests for the many comparisons in a table, with a false discovery rate correction by default (the setting is under Table settings). The automatic scan of an aggregated table and a banner plan against raw data apply no such correction: the risk that testing more things makes something look significant by chance is disclosed every time, via the uncorrected_multiple_comparisons caveat, rather than corrected away.

sections.heading: Output isn't perfectly identical on every rerun
sections.text: The judgment-type steps, clustering related findings, scoring quality, assigning a verdict, are set to run with minimal randomness, which sharply reduces run-to-run variation on the same material. It does not guarantee byte-for-byte identical output every time: large hosted AI models retain a small amount of residual variation in how requests are processed. The honest claim is "much more consistent," not "perfectly deterministic."

sections.heading: Extraction can still make mistakes
sections.text:
Reading a narrative document for claims is a genuinely hard task, and it is done by an AI model, not a fixed parser. It is good at this, not infallible. This is the actual reason every finding starts as pending rather than accepted, and why a human review step exists at all: it is the real safeguard, not a formality.
Why it works this way
Every item on this page is a real, specific boundary, not a blanket disclaimer. Each one is tied to a caveat, a status field, or a described future piece of work you can track, rather than a vague "AI can be wrong" warning that tells you nothing about where to actually be careful.

pages.title: Glossary
pages.blurb: Every term used in this manual, in one place

sections.heading: Introduction
sections.text:
Glossary
Every term used across this manual, in one place, for a quick lookup.
FindingOne atomic, factual or statistical claim extracted from a document or table, with a link back to its exact source.
Pre-insightOne insight per verified, accepted finding. The full, one-to-one audit-trail layer, nothing grouped or reframed yet.
Synthesized insightA smaller number of higher-level, cross-cutting insights, each produced by grouping and reframing a cluster of related pre-insights.
VerdictThe outcome of checking a finding: robust, use with caution, not supported, or insufficient information.
CaveatA specific, named limitation attached to a finding, such as a small base size or an unstated sampling method. See the verification page for the full list.
Ingestion typeWhether an uploaded table is raw (one row per respondent) or aggregated (already summarised). Decides whether the table is scanned automatically or waits for a banner plan.
Banner columnIn a banner plan, a column you name as a segmenting variable (e.g. Gender, Age band) whose categories get compared against each other.
Stub columnIn a banner plan, a column you name as an outcome measure, tested across each banner column's categories.
Entry pointGenerate (start from raw data with no existing findings) or Validate (start from a report that already makes claims).
Status (pending / accepted / rejected)Where a finding, insight, or recommendation sits in human review. Pending means not yet reviewed; rejected moves it to history rather than deleting it.
